entries.cd0020b141dded5903e7144b44a790ad223cf8e7: <div sID="gen5515" type="x-p"/> <chapter n="14" osisID="1Sam.14" sID="1Sam.14"/> <div eID="gen5515" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5516" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen5517" type="x-p"/> We left the host of Israel in a very ill posture, in the close of the foregoing chapter; we saw in them no wisdom, nor strength, nor goodness, to give us ground to expect any other than that they should all be cut off by the army of the Philistines; yet here we find that infinite power which works without means, and that infinite goodness which gives without merit, glorified in a happy turn to their affairs, that still Samuel's words may be made good: "The Lord will not forsake his people, for his great name's sake," (<reference osisRef="1Sam.12.22">ch. xii. 22</reference>. In this chapter we have, I. The host of the Philistines trampled upon, and triumphed over, by the faith and courage of Jonathan, who unknown to his father (<reference osisRef="1Sam.14.1-1Sam.14.3">ver. 1-3</reference>), with his armour-bearer only, made a brave attack upon them, encouraging himself in the Lord his God, <reference osisRef="1Sam.14.4-1Sam.14.7">ver. 4-7</reference>. He challenged them (<reference osisRef="1Sam.14.8-1Sam.14.12">ver. 8-12</reference>), and, upon their acceptance of the challenge, charged them with such fury, or rather such faith, that he put them to flight, and set them one against another (<reference osisRef="1Sam.14.13-1Sam.14.14">ver. 13-15</reference>), which gave opportunity to Saul and his forces, with other Israelites, to follow the blow, and gain a victory, <reference osisRef="1Sam.14.16-1Sam.14.23">ver. 16-23</reference>. II. The host of Israel troubled and perplexed by the rashness and folly of Saul, who adjured the people to eat no food till night, which 1. Brought Jonathan to a præmunire, <reference osisRef="1Sam.14.24-1Sam.14.30">ver. 24-30</reference>. 2. Was a temptation to the people, when the time of their fast had expired, to eat with the blood, <reference osisRef="1Sam.14.31-1Sam.14.35">ver. 31-35</reference>. Jonathan's error, through ignorance, had like to have been his death, but the people rescued him, <reference osisRef="1Sam.14.36-1Sam.14.46">ver. 36-46</reference>. III. In the close we have a general account of Saul's exploits (<reference osisRef="1Sam.14.47-1Sam.14.48">ver. 47, 48</reference>) and of his family, <reference osisRef="1Sam.14.49-1Sam.14.52">ver. 49-52</reference>.
entries.9997b982719209146abfeceb5a116750b585cdeb: <div eID="gen5517" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen5516" type="introduction"/> <title type="x-s3">Jonathan Smites the Philistines. (<hi type="small-caps">b. c.</hi> 1067.)</title> <div sID="gen5518" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">1</hi> Now it came to pass upon a day, that Jonathan the son of Saul said unto the young man that bare his armour, Come, and let us go over to the Philistines' garrison, that <hi type="italic">is</hi> on the other side. But he told not his father. <hi type="super">2</hi> And Saul tarried in the uttermost part of Gibeah under a pomegranate tree which <hi type="italic">is</hi> in Migron: and the people that <hi type="italic">were</hi> with him <hi type="italic">were</hi> about six hundred men; <hi type="super">3</hi> And Ahiah, the son of Ahitub, Ichabod's brother, the son of Phinehas, the son of Eli, the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> 's priest in Shiloh, wearing an ephod. And the people knew not that Jonathan was gone. <hi type="super">4</hi> And between the passages, by which Jonathan sought to go over unto the Philistines' garrison, <hi type="italic">there was</hi> a sharp rock on the one side, and a sharp rock on the other side: and the name of the one <hi type="italic">was</hi> Bozez, and the name of the other Seneh. <hi type="super">5</hi> The forefront of the one <hi type="italic">was</hi> situate northward over against Michmash, and the other southward over against Gibeah. <hi type="super">6</hi> And Jonathan said to the young man that bare his armour, Come, and let us go over unto the garrison of these uncircumcised: it may be that the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> will work for us: for <hi type="italic">there is</hi> no restraint to the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> to save by many or by few. <hi type="super">7</hi> And his armourbearer said unto him, Do all that <hi type="italic">is</hi> in thine heart: turn thee; behold, I <hi type="italic">am</hi> with thee according to thy heart. <hi type="super">8</hi> Then said Jonathan, Behold, we will pass over unto <hi type="italic">these</hi> men, and we will discover ourselves unto them. <hi type="super">9</hi> If they say thus unto us, Tarry until we come to you; then we will stand still in our place, and will not go up unto them. <hi type="super">10</hi> But if they say thus, Come up unto us; then we will go up: for the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> hath delivered them into our hand: and this <hi type="italic">shall be</hi> a sign unto us. <hi type="super">11</hi> And both of them discovered themselves unto the garrison of the Philistines: and the Philistines said, Behold, the Hebrews come forth out of the holes where they had hid themselves. <hi type="super">12</hi> And the men of the garrison answered Jonathan and his armourbearer, and said, Come up to us, and we will shew you a thing. And Jonathan said unto his armourbearer, Come up after me: for the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> hath delivered them into the hand of Israel. <hi type="super">13</hi> And Jonathan climbed up upon his hands and upon his feet, and his armourbearer after him: and they fell before Jonathan; and his armourbearer slew after him. <hi type="super">14</hi> And that first slaughter, which Jonathan and his armourbearer made, was about twenty men, within as it were an half acre of land, <hi type="italic">which</hi> a yoke <hi type="italic">of oxen might plow.</hi> <hi type="super">15</hi> And there was trembling in the host, in the field, and among all the people: the garrison, and the spoilers, they also trembled, and the earth quaked: so it was a very great trembling. <div eID="gen5518" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5519" type="x-p"/> We must here take notice, <div eID="gen5519" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5520" type="x-p"/> I. Of the goodness of God in restraining the Philistines, who had a vast army of valiant men in the field, from falling upon that little handful of timorous trembling people that Saul had with him, whom they would easily have swallowed up at once. It is an invisible power that sets bounds to the malice of the church's enemies, and suffers them not to do that which we should think there is nothing to hinder them from. <div eID="gen5520" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5521" type="x-p"/> II. Of the weakness of Saul, who seems here to have been quite at a loss, and unable to help himself. 1. He pitched his tent under a tree, and had but 600 men with him, <reference osisRef="1Sam.14.2">v. 2</reference>. Where were now the 3000 men he had chosen, and put such a confidence in? <reference osisRef="1Sam.13.2">ch. xiii. 2</reference>. Those whom he trusted too much to failed him when he most needed them. He durst not stay in Gibeah, but got into some obscure place, in the uttermost part of the city, under a pomegranate-tree, under <hi type="italic">Rimmon</hi> (so the word is), <hi type="italic">Ha-Rimmon,</hi> that Rimmon near Gibeah, in the caves of which those 600 Benjamites that escaped his themselves, <reference osisRef="Judg.20.47">Judg. xx. 47</reference>. Some think that there Saul took shelter, so mean and abject was his spirit, now that he had fallen under God's displeasure, every hour expecting the Philistines upon him, and thereby the accomplishment of Samuel's threatening, <reference osisRef="1Sam.13.14">ch. xiii. 14</reference>. Those can never think themselves safe that see themselves cast out of God's protection. 2. Now he sent for a priest, and the ark, a priest from Shiloh, and the ark from Kirjath-jearim, <reference osisRef="1Sam.14.3">v. 3</reference>, <reference osisRef="1Sam.14.18">18</reference>. Saul had once offended by offering sacrifice himself, <reference osisRef="1Sam.13.9">ch. xiii. 9</reference>. Now he resolves never to fall into that error again, and therefore sends for a priest, and hopes to compromise the matter with God Almighty by a particular reformation, as many do whose hearts are unhumbled and unchanged. Samuel, the Lord's prophet, had forsaken him, but he thinks he can make up that loss by commanding Ahiah, the Lord's priest, to attend him, and <hi type="italic">he</hi> will not make him stay for him nor reprove him, as Samuel had done, but will do just as he bids him, <reference osisRef="1Sam.14.18-1Sam.14.19">v. 18, 19</reference>. Many love to have such ministers as will be what they would have them to be, and prophesy smooth things to them; and their caressing them because they are priests, they hope, will atone for their enmity to those ministers that deal faithfully and plainly with them. He will also have the ark brought, perhaps to upbraid Samuel, who in the days of his government, for aught that appears, had not made any public use of it; or in hopes that this would make up the deficiency of his forces; one would have supposed that they would never bring the ark into the camp again, since, the last time, it not only did not save them, but did itself fall into the Philistines' hands. But it is common for those that have lost the substance of religion to be most fond of the shadows of it, as here is a deserted prince courting a deserted priest. <div eID="gen5521" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5522" type="x-p"/> III. Of the bravery and piety of Jonathan, the son of Saul, who was much fitter than the father to wear the crown. "A sweet imp (says bishop Hall) out of a crab-stock." <div eID="gen5522" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5523" type="x-p"/> 1. He resolved to go <hi type="italic">incognito</hi>—<hi type="italic">unknown to any one,</hi> into the camp of the Philistines; he did not acquaint his father with his design, for he knew he would forbid him; nor the people, for he knew they would all discourage him, and, because he resolved not to heed their objections, he resolved not to hear them, nor ask their advice, <reference osisRef="1Sam.14.1">v. 1</reference>, <reference osisRef="1Sam.14.3">3</reference>. Nor had he so great an opinion of the priest as to consult him, but, being conscious of a divine impulse putting him upon it, he threw himself into the mouth of danger, in hope of doing service to his country. The way of access to the enemies' camp is described (<reference osisRef="1Sam.14.4-1Sam.14.5">v. 4, 5</reference>) as being peculiarly difficult, and their natural entrenchments impregnable, yet this does not discourage him; the strength and sharpness of the rocks do but harden and whet his resolutions. Great and generous souls are animated by opposition and take a pleasure in breaking through it. <div eID="gen5523" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5524" type="x-p"/> 2. He encouraged his armour-bearer, a young man that attended him, to go along with him in the daring enterprise, (<reference osisRef="1Sam.14.6">v. 6</reference>): "<hi type="italic">Come, and let us</hi> put our lives in our hands, <hi type="italic">and go over to the</hi> enemies' <hi type="italic">garrison,</hi> and try what we can do to put them into confusion." See whence he draws his encouragements. (1.) "They are uncircumcised, and have not the seal of the covenant in their flesh, as we have. Fear not, we shall do well enough with them, for they are not under the protection of God's covenant as we are, cannot call him theirs as we can, by the sign of circumcision." If such as are enemies to us are also strangers to God, we need not fear them. (2.) "God is able to make us two victorious over their unnumbered regiments. <hi type="italic">There is no restraint in the Lord,</hi> no limitation to the holy One of Israel, but it is all one to him <hi type="italic">to save by many or by few.</hi>" This is a true easily granted in general, that it is all alike to Omnipotence what the instruments are by which it works; and yet it is not so easy to apply it to a particular case; when we are but few and feeble then to believe that God can not only save us, but save by us, this is an instance of faith, which, wherever it is, shall obtain a good report. Let this strengthen the weak and encourage the timid: let it be pleaded with God for the enforcing of our petitions and with ourselves for the silencing of our fears: <hi type="italic">It is nothing with God to help, whether with many or with those that have no power,</hi> <reference osisRef="2Chr.14.11">2 Chron. xiv. 11</reference>. (3.) "Who knows but he that can use us for his glory will do it? <hi type="italic">It may be the Lord will work for us,</hi> work with us, work a sign or miracle for us." So the Chaldee. We may encourage ourselves with hope that God will appear for us, though we have not ground on which to build an assurance. An active faith will venture far in God's cause upon an <hi type="italic">it may be.</hi> Jonathan's armour-bearer, or esquire, as if he had learned to carry, not his arms only, but his heart, promised to stand by him and to follow him whithersoever he went, <reference osisRef="1Sam.14.7">v. 7</reference>. We have reason to think that Jonathan felt a divine impulse and impression putting him upon this bold adventure, in which he was encouraged by his servant's concurrence, otherwise the danger was so great which he ran upon that he would have tempted God rather than trusted him. And perhaps he had an actual regard to that word of Joshua (<reference osisRef="Josh.23.10">Josh. xxiii. 10</reference>), <hi type="italic">One man of you shall chase a thousand,</hi> borrowed from Moses, <reference osisRef="Deut.32.30">Deut. xxxii. 30</reference>. <div eID="gen5524" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5525" type="x-p"/> 3. How bold soever his resolution was, he resolved to follow Providence in the execution of it, which, he believed, would guide him <hi type="italic">with its eye</hi> (<reference osisRef="Ps.32.8">Ps. xxxii. 8</reference>), and which therefore he would carefully attend and take hints of direction from. See how he put himself upon Providence, and resolved to be determined by it. "Come" (says he to his confidant), "we will discover ourselves to the enemy, as those that are not afraid to look them in the face (<reference osisRef="1Sam.14.8">v. 8</reference>), and then, if they be so cautious as to bid us stand, we will advance no further, taking it for an intimation of Providence that God would have us act defensively, and we will prepare as well as we can to give them a warm reception (<reference osisRef="1Sam.14.9">v. 9</reference>); but if they be so presumptuous as to challenge us, and the first sentinel we meet with bid us march on, we will push forward, and make as brisk an onset, assuredly gathering thence that it is the will of God we should act offensively, and then not doubting but he will <hi type="italic">stand by us,</hi>" <reference osisRef="1Sam.14.10">v. 10</reference>. And upon this issue he puts it, firmly believing, as we all should, (1.) That God has the governing of the hearts and tongues of all men, even of those that know him not, nor have any regard to him, and serves his own purposes by them, though they mean not so, neither do their hearts think so. Jonathan knew God could discover his mind to him if he pleased, and would do it, since he depended upon him, as surely by the mouth of a Philistine as by the mouth of a priest. (2.) That God will, some way or other, direct the steps of those that <hi type="italic">acknowledge him in all their ways,</hi> and seek unto him for direction, with full purpose of heart to follow it. Sometimes we find most comfort in that which is least our own doing, and into which we have been led by the unexpected, but well observed, turns of Providence. <div eID="gen5525" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5526" type="x-p"/> 4. Providence gave him the sign he expected, and he answered the signal. He and his armour-bearer did not surprise the Philistines when they were asleep, but discovered themselves to them by day-light, <reference osisRef="1Sam.14.11">v. 11</reference>. The guards of the Philistines, (1.) Disdained them, upbraided them with the cowardice of many of their people, and looked upon them to be of the regiment of sneakers: <hi type="italic">Behold, the Hebrews come forth out of their holes.</hi> If some of Christ's soldiers play the coward, others that play the man may perhaps be upbraided with it. (2.) They defied them (<reference osisRef="1Sam.14.12">v. 12</reference>): <hi type="italic">Come, and we will show you a thing,</hi> as if they came like children to gaze about them; but meaning, as Goliath (<reference osisRef="1Sam.17.44">ch. xvii. 44</reference>), that they would <hi type="italic">give them as meat to the fowls of the air.</hi> They bantered them, not doubting but to make a prey of them. This greatly emboldened Jonathan. With it he encouraged his servant; he had spoken with uncertainty (<reference osisRef="1Sam.14.6">v. 6</reference>): <hi type="italic">It may be the Lord will work for us;</hi> but now he speaks with assurance (<reference osisRef="1Sam.14.12">v. 12</reference>): <hi type="italic">The Lord has delivered them,</hi> not into our hands (he sought not his own glory), but <hi type="italic">into the hand of Israel,</hi> for he aimed at nothing but the advantage of the public. His faith being thus strengthened, no difficulty can stand before him; he climbs up the rock upon all four (<reference osisRef="1Sam.14.13">v. 13</reference>), though he has nothing to cover him, nor any but his own servant to second him, nor any human probability of any thing but death before him. <div eID="gen5526" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5527" type="x-p"/> 5. The wonderful success of this daring enterprise. The Philistines, instead of falling upon Jonathan, to slay him, or take him prisoner, fell before him (<reference osisRef="1Sam.14.13">v. 13</reference>) unaccountably, upon the first blows he gave. They fell, that is, (1.) They were many of them slain by him and his armour-bearer, <reference osisRef="1Sam.14.14">v. 14</reference>. Twenty Philistines fell presently. It was not so much the name of Jonathan that made them yield so tamely (though some think that this had become terrible to them, since he smote one of their garrisons, <reference osisRef="1Sam.13.3">ch. xiii. 3</reference>), but it was God's right hand and his arm that got him this victory. (2.) The rest were put to flight, and fell foul upon one another (<reference osisRef="1Sam.14.15">v. 15</reference>): <hi type="italic">There was trembling in the host.</hi> There was no visible cause for fear; they were so numerous, bold, and advantageously posted; the Israelites had fled before them; not an enemy made head against them, but one gentleman and his man; and yet they shook like an aspen-leaf. The consternation was general: they all trembled; even <hi type="italic">the spoilers,</hi> those that had been most bold and forward, shared in the common fright, the joints of their loins were loosed, and their knees smote one against another, and yet none of them could tell why or wherefore. It is called <hi type="italic">a trembling of God</hi> (so the original phrase is), signifying not only, as we render it, a very great trembling, which they could not resist nor reason themselves clear of, but that it was supernatural, and came immediately from the hand of God. He that made the heart knows how to make it tremble. To complete the confusion, even the earth quaked, and made them ready to fear that it would sink under them. Those that will not fear the eternal God, he can make afraid of a shadow. See <reference osisRef="Prov.21.1">Prov. xxi. 1</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.33.14">Isa. xxxiii. 14</reference>.
entries.7d7cffe02d2095b62786c5fb4aa5fbfb4e5e16d3: <div eID="gen5527" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">The Philistines Destroyed. (<hi type="small-caps">b. c.</hi> 1067.)</title> <div sID="gen5528" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">16</hi> And the watchmen of Saul in Gibeah of Benjamin looked; and, behold, the multitude melted away, and they went on beating down <hi type="italic">one another.</hi> <hi type="super">17</hi> Then said Saul unto the people that <hi type="italic">were</hi> with him, Number now, and see who is gone from us. And when they had numbered, behold, Jonathan and his armourbearer <hi type="italic">were</hi> not <hi type="italic">there.</hi> <hi type="super">18</hi> And Saul said unto Ahiah, Bring hither the ark of God. For the ark of God was at that time with the children of Israel. <hi type="super">19</hi> And it came to pass, while Saul talked unto the priest, that the noise that <hi type="italic">was</hi> in the host of the Philistines went on and increased: and Saul said unto the priest, Withdraw thine hand. <hi type="super">20</hi> And Saul and all the people that <hi type="italic">were</hi> with him assembled themselves, and they came to the battle: and, behold, every man's sword was against his fellow, <hi type="italic">and there was</hi> a very great discomfiture. <hi type="super">21</hi> Moreover the Hebrews <hi type="italic">that</hi> were with the Philistines before that time, which went up with them into the camp <hi type="italic">from the country</hi> round about, even they also <hi type="italic">turned</hi> to be with the Israelites that <hi type="italic">were</hi> with Saul and Jonathan. <hi type="super">22</hi> Likewise all the men of Israel which had hid themselves in mount Ephraim, <hi type="italic">when</hi> they heard that the Philistines fled, even they also followed hard after them in the battle. <hi type="super">23</hi> So the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> saved Israel that day: and the battle passed over unto Beth-aven. <div eID="gen5528" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5529" type="x-p"/> We have here the prosecution and improvement of the wonderful advantages which Jonathan and his armour-bearer gained against the Philistines. <div eID="gen5529" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5530" type="x-p"/> I. The Philistines were, by the power of God, set against one another. They melted away like snow before the sun, and <hi type="italic">went on beating down one another</hi> (<reference osisRef="1Sam.14.16">v. 16</reference>), for (<reference osisRef="1Sam.14.20">v. 20</reference>) <hi type="italic">every man's sword was against his fellow.</hi> When they fled for fear, instead of turning back upon those that chased them, they reckoned those only their enemies that stood in their way, and treated them accordingly. The Philistines were very secure, because all the swords and spears were in their hands. Israel had none except what Saul and Jonathan had. But now God showed them the folly of that confidence, by making their own swords and spears the instruments of their own destruction, and more fatal in their own hands than if they had been in the hands of Israel. See the like done, <reference osisRef="Judg.7.22">Judg. vii. 22</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Chr.20.23">2 Chron. xx. 23</reference>. <div eID="gen5530" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5531" type="x-p"/> II. The Israelites were hereby animated against them. <div eID="gen5531" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5532" type="x-p"/> 1. Notice was soon taken of it by the watchmen of Saul, those that stood sentinel at Gibeah, <reference osisRef="1Sam.14.16">v. 16</reference>. They were aware that the host of the enemy was in great confusion, and that a great slaughter was made among them, and yet, upon search, they found none of their own forces absent, but only Jonathan and his servant (<reference osisRef="1Sam.14.17">v. 17</reference>), which no doubt greatly animated them, and assured them that it could be no other than the Lord's doing, when there was no more of man's doing than what those two could do against a great host. <div eID="gen5532" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5533" type="x-p"/> 2. Saul began to enquire of God, but soon desisted. His spirit had not come down so far as to allow him to consult Samuel, though, it is probable, he was near him; for we read (<reference osisRef="1Sam.13.15">ch. xiii. 15</reference>) that he had come to Gibeah of Benjamin; but he called for the ark (<reference osisRef="1Sam.14.18">v. 18</reference>), desiring to know whether it would be safe for him to attack the Philistines, upon the disorder they perceived them to be in. Many will consult God about their safety that would never consult him about their duty. But, perceiving by his scouts that the noise in the enemy's camp increased, he commanded the priest that officiated to break off abruptly: "<hi type="italic">Withdraw thy hand</hi> (<reference osisRef="1Sam.14.19">v. 19</reference>), consult no more, wait no longer for an answer." He was very unwise indeed if (as some think) he forbade him to lift up his hands in prayer; for when Joshua was actually engaged with Amalek Moses continued still to lift up his hands. It is rather a prohibition to his enquiring of the Lord, either, (1.) Because now he thought he did not need an answer, the case was plain enough. And yet the more evident it was that God did all the more reason he had to enquire whether he would give him leave to do any thing. Or, (2.) Because now he would not stay for it; he was in such haste to fight a falling enemy that he would not stay to make and end of his devotions, nor hear what answer God would give him. A little thing will divert a vain and carnal mind from religious exercises. He that believeth will not make haste, such haste as this, nor reckon any business so urgent as not to allow time to take God along with him. <div eID="gen5533" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5534" type="x-p"/> 3. He, and all the little force he had, made a vigorous attack upon the enemy; and all the people <hi type="italic">were cried together</hi> (so the word is, <reference osisRef="1Sam.14.20">v. 20</reference>), for want of the silver trumpets wherewith God appointed them to sound an alarm in the day of battle, <reference osisRef="Num.10.9">Num. x. 9</reference>. They summoned them together by shouting, and their number was not so great but that they might soon be got together. And now they seem bold and brave when the work is done to their hands. Our Lord Jesus had conquered our spiritual enemies, routed and dispersed them, so that we are cowards indeed if we will not stand to our arms when it is only to pursue the victory and to divide the spoil. <div eID="gen5534" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5535" type="x-p"/> 4. Every Hebrew, even those from whom one would least have expected it, now turned his hand against the Philistines. (1.) Those that had deserted and gone over to the enemy, and were among them, now fought against them, <reference osisRef="1Sam.14.21">v. 21</reference>. Some think, they were such as had been taken prisoners by them, and now they were goads in their sides. It rather seems that they went in to them voluntarily, but, now that they saw them falling, recovered the hearts of Israelites, and did valiantly for their country. (2.) Those that had fled their colours, and hid themselves in the mountains, returned to their posts, and joined in with the pursuers (<reference osisRef="1Sam.14.22">v. 22</reference>), hoping by their great zeal and officiousness, now that the danger was over and the victory sure, to atone for their former cowardice. It was not much to their praise to appear now, but it would have been more their reproach if they had not appeared. Those that are remiss and faint-hearted indeed that will not act in the cause of God when they see it victorious, as well as righteous. Thus all hands were at work against the Philistines, and every Israelite slew as many as he could, without sword or spear; yet it is said (<reference osisRef="1Sam.14.23">v. 23</reference>), it <hi type="italic">was the Lord that saved Israel that day.</hi> He did it by them, for without him they could do nothing. <hi type="italic">Salvation is of the Lord.</hi>
entries.b5cf274c9d454baf5f6b348bd2a3860d3225dfa6: <div eID="gen5535" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">Saul's Rash Oath. (<hi type="small-caps">b. c.</hi> 1067.)</title> <div sID="gen5536" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">24</hi> And the men of Israel were distressed that day: for Saul had adjured the people, saying, Cursed <hi type="italic">be</hi> the man that eateth <hi type="italic">any</hi> food until evening, that I may be avenged on mine enemies. So none of the people tasted <hi type="italic">any</hi> food. <hi type="super">25</hi> And all <hi type="italic">they of</hi> the land came to a wood; and there was honey upon the ground. <hi type="super">26</hi> And when the people were come into the wood, behold, the honey dropped; but no man put his hand to his mouth: for the people feared the oath. <hi type="super">27</hi> But Jonathan heard not when his father charged the people with the oath: wherefore he put forth the end of the rod that <hi type="italic">was</hi> in his hand, and dipped it in a honeycomb, and put his hand to his mouth; and his eyes were enlightened. <hi type="super">28</hi> Then answered one of the people, and said, Thy father straitly charged the people with an oath, saying, Cursed <hi type="italic">be</hi> the man that eateth <hi type="italic">any</hi> food this day. And the people were faint. <hi type="super">29</hi> Then said Jonathan, My father hath troubled the land: see, I pray you, how mine eyes have been enlightened, because I tasted a little of this honey. <hi type="super">30</hi> How much more, if haply the people had eaten freely to day of the spoil of their enemies which they found? for had there not been now a much greater slaughter among the Philistines? <hi type="super">31</hi> And they smote the Philistines that day from Michmash to Aijalon: and the people were very faint. <hi type="super">32</hi> And the people flew upon the spoil, and took sheep, and oxen, and calves, and slew <hi type="italic">them</hi> on the ground: and the people did eat <hi type="italic">them</hi> with the blood. <hi type="super">33</hi> Then they told Saul, saying, Behold, the people sin against the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> , in that they eat with the blood. And he said, Ye have transgressed: roll a great stone unto me this day. <hi type="super">34</hi> And Saul said, Disperse yourselves among the people, and say unto them, Bring me hither every man his ox, and every man his sheep, and slay <hi type="italic">them</hi> here, and eat; and sin not against the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> in eating with the blood. And all the people brought every man his ox with him that night, and slew <hi type="italic">them</hi> there. <hi type="super">35</hi> And Saul built an altar unto the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> : the same was the first altar that he built unto the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> . <div eID="gen5536" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5537" type="x-p"/> We have here an account of the distress of the children of Israel, even in the day of their triumphs. Such alloys are all present joys subject to. And such obstructions does many a good cause meet with, even when it seems most prosperous, through the mismanagement of instruments. <div eID="gen5537" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5538" type="x-p"/> I. Saul forbade the people, under the penalty of a curse, to taste any food that day, <reference osisRef="1Sam.14.24">v. 24</reference>. Here we will suppose, 1. That as king he had power to put his soldiers under this interdict, and to bind it on with a curse; and therefore they submitted to it, and God so far owned it as to discover, by the lot, that Jonathan was the delinquent that had meddled with the accursed thing (though ignorantly), on which account God would not be at that time enquired of by them. 2. That he did it with a good intention, lest the people, who perhaps had been kept for some time at short allowance, when they found plenty of victuals in the deserted camp of the Philistines, should fall greedily upon that, and so lose time in pursing the enemy, and some of them, it may be, glut themselves to such a degree as not to be fit for any more service that day. To prevent this, he forbade them to taste any food, and laid himself, it is likely, under the same restraint. And yet his making this severe order was, (1.) Impolitic and very unwise; for, if it gained time, it lost strength, for the pursuit. (2.) It was imperious, and disobliging to the people, and worse than <hi type="italic">muzzling the mouth of the ox when he treads out the corn.</hi> To forbid them to feast would have been commendable, but to forbid them so much as to taste, though ever so hungry, was barbarous. (3.) It was impious to enforce the prohibition with a curse and an oath. Had he no penalty less than an anathema wherewith to support his military discipline? Death for such a crime would have been too much, but especially death with a curse. Though superiors may chide and correct, they may not curse their inferiors; our rule is, <hi type="italic">Bless, and curse not.</hi> When David speaks of an enemy he had that loved cursing perhaps he meant Saul, <reference osisRef="Ps.109.17-Ps.109.18">Ps. cix. 17, 18</reference>. <div eID="gen5538" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5539" type="x-p"/> II. The people observed his order, but it had many inconveniences attending it. 1. The soldiers were tantalized; for, in their pursuit of the enemy, it happened that they went through a wood so full of wild honey that it dropped from the trees upon the ground, the Philistines having perhaps, in their flight, broken in upon the honeycombs, for their own refreshment, and left them running. Canaan flowed with honey, and here is an instance of it. They sucked honey out of <hi type="italic">the rock, the flinty rock</hi> (<reference osisRef="Deut.32.13">Deut. xxxii. 13</reference>); yet, for fear of the curse, they did not so much as taste the honey, <reference osisRef="1Sam.14.25-1Sam.14.26">v. 25, 26</reference>. Those are worthy of the name of Israelites that can deny themselves and their own appetites even when they are most craving, and the delights of sense most tempting, for fear of guilt and a curse, and the table becoming a snare. Let us never feed ourselves, much less feast ourselves, without fear. 2. Jonathan fell under the curse through ignorance. He heard not of the charge his father had given; for, having bravely forced the lines, he was then following the chase, and therefore might justly be looked upon as exempted from the charge and intended in it. But it seems it was taken for granted, and he himself did not object against it afterwards, that it extended to him, though absent upon so good an occasion. He, not knowing any peril in it, took up a piece of a honey-comb, upon the end of his staff, and sucked it (<reference osisRef="1Sam.14.27">v. 27</reference>), and was sensibly refreshed by it: <hi type="italic">His eyes were enlightened,</hi> which began to grow dim through hunger and faintness; it made his countenance look pleasant and cheerful, for it was such as a stander-by might discern (<reference osisRef="1Sam.14.29">v. 29</reference>): <hi type="italic">See how my eyes have been enlightened.</hi> He thought no harm, nor feared any, till one of the people acquainted him with the order, and then he found himself in a snare. Many a good son has been thus entangled and distressed, in more ways than one, by the rashness of an inconsiderate father. Jonathan, for his part, lost the crown he was heir to by his father's folly, which, it may be, this was an ill omen of. 3. The soldiers were faint, and grew feeble, in the pursuit of the Philistines. Jonathan foresaw this would be the effect of it; their spirits would flag, and their strength would fail, for want of sustenance. Such is the nature of our bodies that they soon grow unfit for service if they be not supplied with fresh recruits. Daily work cannot be done without daily bread, which our Father in heaven graciously gives us. It is <hi type="italic">bread</hi> that <hi type="italic">strengthens man's heart;</hi> therefore Jonathan reasoned very well, <hi type="italic">If the people had eaten freely,</hi> there would have been <hi type="italic">a much greater slaughter</hi> (<reference osisRef="1Sam.14.30">v. 30</reference>); but, as it was, they were <hi type="italic">very faint, too much fatigued</hi> (so the Chaldee), and began to think more of their meat than of their work. 4. The worst effect of all was that at evening, when the restraint was taken off and they returned to their food again, they were so greedy and eager upon it that they ate the flesh with the blood, expressly contrary to the law of God, <reference osisRef="1Sam.14.32">v. 32</reference>. Two hungry meals, we say, make the third a glutton; it was so here. They would not stay to have their meat either duly killed (for they slew the cattle upon the ground, and did not hang them up, as they used to do, that the blood might all run out of them) or duly dressed, but fell greedily upon it before it was half boiled or half roasted, <reference osisRef="1Sam.14.32">v. 32</reference>. Saul, being informed of it, reproved them for the sin (<reference osisRef="1Sam.14.33">v. 33</reference>): <hi type="italic">You have transgressed;</hi> but did not, as he should have done, reflect upon himself as having been accessory to it, and having <hi type="italic">made the Lord's people to transgress.</hi> To put a stop to this irregularity, Saul ordered them to set up a great stone before him, and let all that had cattle to kill, for their present use, bring them thither, and kill them under his eye upon that stone (<reference osisRef="1Sam.14.33">v. 33</reference>), and the people did so (<reference osisRef="1Sam.14.34">v. 34</reference>), so easily were they restrained and reformed when their prince took care to do his part. If magistrates would but use their power as they might, people would be made better than they are with more ease than is imagined. <div eID="gen5539" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5540" type="x-p"/> III. On this occasion Saul built an altar (<reference osisRef="1Sam.14.35">v. 35</reference>), that he might offer sacrifice, either by way of acknowledgment of the victory they had obtained or by the way of atonement for the sin they had been guilty of. <hi type="italic">The same was the first altar that he built,</hi> and perhaps the rolling of the great stone to kill the beasts on reminded him of converting it into an altar, else he would not have thought of it. Saul was turning aside from God, and yet now he began to build altars, being most zealous (as many are) for the form of godliness when he was denying the power of it. See <reference osisRef="Hos.8.14">Hos. viii. 14</reference>, <hi type="italic">Israel has forgotten his Maker, and buildeth temples.</hi> Some read it, <hi type="italic">He began to build that altar;</hi> he laid the first stone, but was so hasty to pursue his victory that he could not stay to finish it.
entries.ea314cc7a0d01dc6ccb36eff88012753f60cafe8: <div eID="gen5540" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">Jonathan Condemned to Die; Jonathan Rescued. (<hi type="small-caps">b. c.</hi> 1067.)</title> <div sID="gen5541" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">36</hi> And Saul said, Let us go down after the Philistines by night, and spoil them until the morning light, and let us not leave a man of them. And they said, Do whatsoever seemeth good unto thee. Then said the priest, Let us draw near hither unto God. <hi type="super">37</hi> And Saul asked counsel of God, Shall I go down after the Philistines? wilt thou deliver them into the hand of Israel? But he answered him not that day. <hi type="super">38</hi> And Saul said, Draw ye near hither, all the chief of the people: and know and see wherein this sin hath been this day. <hi type="super">39</hi> For, <hi type="italic">as</hi> the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> liveth, which saveth Israel, though it be in Jonathan my son, he shall surely die. But <hi type="italic">there was</hi> not a man among all the people <hi type="italic">that</hi> answered him. <hi type="super">40</hi> Then said he unto all Israel, Be ye on one side, and I and Jonathan my son will be on the other side. And the people said unto Saul, Do what seemeth good unto thee. <hi type="super">41</hi> Therefore Saul said unto the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> God of Israel, Give a perfect <hi type="italic">lot.</hi> And Saul and Jonathan were taken: but the people escaped. <hi type="super">42</hi> And Saul said, Cast <hi type="italic">lots</hi> between me and Jonathan my son. And Jonathan was taken. <hi type="super">43</hi> Then Saul said to Jonathan, Tell me what thou hast done. And Jonathan told him, and said, I did but taste a little honey with the end of the rod that <hi type="italic">was</hi> in mine hand, <hi type="italic">and,</hi> lo, I must die. <hi type="super">44</hi> And Saul answered, God do so and more also: for thou shalt surely die, Jonathan. <hi type="super">45</hi> And the people said unto Saul, Shall Jonathan die, who hath wrought this great salvation in Israel? God forbid: <hi type="italic">as</hi> the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> liveth, there shall not one hair of his head fall to the ground; for he hath wrought with God this day. So the people rescued Jonathan, that he died not. <hi type="super">46</hi> Then Saul went up from following the Philistines: and the Philistines went to their own place. <div eID="gen5541" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5542" type="x-p"/> Here is, I. Saul's boasting against the Philistines. He proposed, as soon as his soldiers had got their suppers, to pursue them all night, and <hi type="italic">not leave a man of them,</hi> <reference osisRef="1Sam.14.36">v. 36</reference>. Here he showed much zeal, but little discretion; for his army, thus fatigued, could as ill spare a night's sleep as a meal's meat. But it is common for rash and foolish men to consider nobody but themselves, and, so that they might but have their humour, not to care what hardships they put upon those that are under them. However, the people were so obsequious to their king that they would by no means oppose the motion, but resolved to make the best of it, and, if he will go on, they will follow him: <hi type="italic">Do whatsoever seemeth good to thee.</hi> Only the priest thought it convenient to go on with the devotions that were broken off abruptly (<reference osisRef="1Sam.14.19">v. 19</reference>), and to consult the oracle: <hi type="italic">Let us draw near hither unto God.</hi> Princes and great men have need of such about them as will thus be their remembrancers, wherever they go, to take God along with them. And, when the priest proposed it, Saul could not for shame reject the proposal, but <hi type="italic">asked counsel of God</hi> (<reference osisRef="1Sam.14.37">v. 37</reference>): "<hi type="italic">Shall I go down after the Philistines?</hi> And shall I speed?" <div eID="gen5542" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5543" type="x-p"/> II. His falling foul on his son Jonathan: and the rest of this paragraph is wholly concerning him: for, while he is prosecuted, the Philistines make their escape. We know not what mischief may ensue upon on rash resolve. <div eID="gen5543" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5544" type="x-p"/> 1. God, by giving an intimation of his displeasure, put Saul upon searching for an accursed thing. When, by the priest, he consulted the oracle, God <hi type="italic">answered him not,</hi> <reference osisRef="1Sam.14.37">v. 37</reference>. Note, When God denies our prayers it concerns us to enquire what the sin is that has provoked him to do so. <hi type="italic">Let us see where the sin is,</hi> <reference osisRef="1Sam.14.38">v. 38</reference>. For God's ear is not heavy that it cannot hear, but it is sin that separates between us and him. If God turns away our prayer, we have reason to suspect it is for some iniquity regarding our hearts, which we are concerned to find out, that we may put it away, may mortify it, and put it to death. Saul swears by his Maker that whoever was the Achan that troubled the camp, by eating the forbidden fruit, should certainly die, though it were Jonathan himself, that is, though ever so dear to himself and the people, little thinking that Jonathan was the man (<reference osisRef="1Sam.14.39">v. 39</reference>): <hi type="italic">He shall surely die,</hi> the curse shall be executed upon him. But none of the people answered him, that is, none of those who knew Jonathan had broken the order would inform against him. <div eID="gen5544" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5545" type="x-p"/> 2. Jonathan was discovered by lot to be the offender. Saul would have lots cast between himself and Jonathan on the one side, and the people on the other, perhaps because he was as confident of Jonathan's innocency in this matter as of his own, <reference osisRef="1Sam.14.40">v. 40</reference>. The people, seeing him in a heat, durst not gainsay any thing he proposed, but acquiesced: <hi type="italic">Do as seemeth good unto thee.</hi> Before he cast lots, he prayed that <hi type="italic">God would give a perfect lot</hi> (<reference osisRef="1Sam.14.41">v. 41</reference>), that is, make a full discovery of this matter, or, as it is in the margin, that he would show the innocent. This was with an air of impartial justice. Judges should desire that truth may come out, whoever may suffer by it. Lots should be cast with prayer, because they are a solemn appeal to Providence, and by them we beg of God to direct and determine us (<reference osisRef="Acts.1.24">Acts i. 24</reference>), for which reason some have condemned games that depend purely upon lot or chance as making too bold with a sacred thing. Jonathan at length was taken (<reference osisRef="1Sam.14.42">v. 42</reference>), Providence designing hereby to countenance and support a lawful authority, and to put an honour upon the administration of public justice in general, reserving another way to bring off one that had done nothing worthy of death. <div eID="gen5545" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5546" type="x-p"/> 3. Jonathan ingenuously confesses the fact, and Saul, with an angry curse, passes sentence upon him. Jonathan denies not the truth, nor goes about to conceal it, only he thinks it hard that he must <hi type="italic">die for it,</hi> <reference osisRef="1Sam.14.43">v. 43</reference>. He might very fairly have pleaded his invincible ignorance of the law, or have insisted upon his merit, but he submitted to the necessity with a great and generous mind: "God's and my father's will be done:" thus he showed as much valour in receiving the messengers of death himself as in sending them among the Philistines. It is as brave to yield in some cases as it is in other cases to fight. Saul is not mollified by his filial submission nor the hardness of his case; but as one that affected to be thought firm to his word, and much more to his oath; even when it bound him hardest, with another imprecation he gives judgment upon Jonathan (<reference osisRef="1Sam.14.44">v. 44</reference>): "<hi type="italic">God do so and more also</hi> to me if I do not execute the law upon thee, <hi type="italic">for thou shalt surely die, Jonathan.</hi>" (1.) He passed this sentence too hastily, without consulting the oracle. Jonathan had a very good plea in arrest of the judgment. What he had done was not <hi type="italic">malum in se</hi>—<hi type="italic">bad in itself;</hi> and, as for the prohibition of it, he was ignorant of that, so that he could not be charged with rebellion or disobedience. (2.) He did it in fury. Had Jonathan been worthy to die, yet it would have become a judge, much more a father, to pass sentence with tenderness and compassion, and not with such an air of triumph, like a man perfectly divested of all humanity and natural affection. Justice is debased when it is administered with wrath and bitterness. (3.) He backed it with a curse upon himself if he did not see the sentence executed; and this curse did return upon his own head. Jonathan escaped, but God did so to Saul, and more also; for he was rejected of God and made anathema. Let none upon any occasion dare to use such imprecations as these, lest God say Amen to them, and <hi type="italic">make their own tongues to fall upon them,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ps.64.8">Ps. lxiv. 8</reference>. This stone will return upon him that rolleth it. Yet we have reason to think that Saul's bowels yearned toward Jonathan, so that he really punished himself, and very justly, when he seemed so severe upon Jonathan. God made him feel the smart of his own rash edict, which might make him fear being again guilty of the like. By all these vexatious accidents God did likewise correct him for his presumption in offering sacrifice without Samuel. An expedition so ill begun could not end without some rebukes. <div eID="gen5546" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5547" type="x-p"/> 4. The people rescued Jonathan out of his father's hands, <reference osisRef="1Sam.14.45">v. 45</reference>. Hitherto they had expressed themselves very observant of Saul. What seemed good to him they acquiesced in, <reference osisRef="1Sam.14.36">v. 36</reference>, <reference osisRef="1Sam.14.40">40</reference>. But, when Jonathan is in danger, Saul's word is no longer a law to them, but with the utmost zeal they oppose the execution of his sentence: "<hi type="italic">Shall Jonathan die</hi>—that blessing, that darling, of his country? Shall that life be sacrificed to a punctilio of law and honour which was so bravely exposed for the public service, and to which we owe our lives and triumphs? No, we will never stand by and see him thus treated whom God delights to honour." It is good to see Israelites zealous for the protection of those whom God has made instruments of public good. Saul had sworn that Jonathan should die, but they oppose their oath to his, and swear he shall not die: "<hi type="italic">As the Lord liveth there shall not</hi> only not his head, but not <hi type="italic">a hair of his head fall to the ground;</hi>" they did not rescue him by violence, but by reason and resolution; and Josephus says they made their prayer to God that he might be loosed from the curse. They pleaded for him that <hi type="italic">he has wrought with God this day;</hi> that is, "he has owned God's cause, and God has owned his endeavours, and therefore his life is too precious to be thrown away upon a nicety." We may suppose Saul had not so perfectly forgotten the relation of a father but that he was willing enough to have Jonathan rescued, and well pleased to have that done which yet he would not do himself: and he that knows the heart of a father knows not how to blame him. <div eID="gen5547" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5548" type="x-p"/> 5. The design against the Philistines is quashed by this incident (<reference osisRef="1Sam.14.46">v. 46</reference>): <hi type="italic">Saul went up from following them,</hi> and so an opportunity was lost of completing the victory. When Israel's shields are clashing with one another the public safety and service suffer by it.
entries.b5d8015ec14b40a6a85106facf76a9a62d9818ae: <div eID="gen5548" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">The Amalekites Destroyed. (<hi type="small-caps">b. c.</hi> 1067.)</title> <div sID="gen5549" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">47</hi> So Saul took the kingdom over Israel, and fought against all his enemies on every side, against Moab, and against the children of Ammon, and against Edom, and against the kings of Zobah, and against the Philistines: and whithersoever he turned himself, he vexed <hi type="italic">them.</hi> <hi type="super">48</hi> And he gathered a host, and smote the Amalekites, and delivered Israel out of the hands of them that spoiled them. <hi type="super">49</hi> Now the sons of Saul were Jonathan, and Ishui, and Melchishua: and the names of his two daughters <hi type="italic">were these;</hi> the name of the firstborn Merab, and the name of the younger Michal: <hi type="super">50</hi> And the name of Saul's wife <hi type="italic">was</hi> Ahinoam, the daughter of Ahimaaz: and the name of the captain of his host <hi type="italic">was</hi> Abner, the son of Ner, Saul's uncle. <hi type="super">51</hi> And Kish <hi type="italic">was</hi> the father of Saul; and Ner the father of Abner <hi type="italic">was</hi> the son of Abiel. <hi type="super">52</hi> And there was sore war against the Philistines all the days of Saul: and when Saul saw any strong man, or any valiant man, he took him unto him. <div eID="gen5549" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5550" type="x-p"/> Here is a general account of Saul's court and camp. 1. Of his court and family, the names of his sons and daughters (<reference osisRef="1Sam.14.49">v. 49</reference>), and of his wife and his cousin-german that was general of his army, <reference osisRef="1Sam.14.50">v. 50</reference>. There is mention of another wife of Saul's (<reference osisRef="2Sam.21.8">2 Sam. xxi. 8</reference>), Rizpah, a secondary wife, and of the children he had by her. 2. Of his camp and military actions. (1.) How he levied his army: <hi type="italic">When he saw any strong valiant man,</hi> that was remarkably fit for service, <hi type="italic">he took him unto him</hi> (<reference osisRef="1Sam.14.52">v. 52</reference>), as Samuel had told them the manner of the king would be (<reference osisRef="1Sam.8.11">ch. viii. 11</reference>); and, if he must have a standing army, it was his prudence to fill it up with the ablest men he could make choice of. (2.) How he employed his army. He guarded his country against the insults of its enemies on every side, and prevented their incursions, <reference osisRef="1Sam.14.47-1Sam.14.48">v. 47, 48</reference>. It is supposed that he acted only defensively against those that used to invade the borders of Israel; <hi type="italic">and whithersoever he turned himself,</hi> as there was occasion, <hi type="italic">he vexed them,</hi> by checking and disappointing them. But the enemies he struggled most with were the Philistines, with whom he had <hi type="italic">sore war all his days,</hi> <reference osisRef="1Sam.14.52">v. 52</reference>. He had little reason to be proud of his royal dignity, nor had any of his neighbours cause to envy him, for he had little enjoyment of himself after he took the kingdom. He could not vex his enemies without some vexation to himself, such thorns are crowns quilted with.  <chapter eID="1Sam.14"/> <div eID="gen5550" type="x-p"/>

entries.4056d1bc920684ffab3c64af1d0f89cd611476c5: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv2618"/><title type="x-s2">CHAPTER 14</title> <div sID="gen3552" type="x-p"/> <reference osisRef="1Sam.14.1-1Sam.14.14">1Sa 14:1-14</reference>. Jonathan Miraculously Smites the Philistines' Garrison.<div eID="gen3552" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3553" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv2618"/><hi type="bold">1. the Philistines' garrison--</hi>"the standing camp" (<reference osisRef="1Sam.13.23">1Sa 13:23</reference>, Margin) "in the passage of Michmash" (<reference osisRef="1Sam.13.16">1Sa 13:16</reference>), now Wady Es-Suweinit. "It begins in the neighborhood of Betin (Beth-el) and El-Bireh (Beetroth), and as it breaks through the ridge below these places, its sides form precipitous walls. On the right, about a quarter of an acre below, it again breaks off, and passes between high perpendicular precipices" [Robinson]. <div eID="gen3553" type="x-p"/>
entries.954422b775cff69beb9111b5993592356930b4fb: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv2619"/><div sID="gen3554" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv2619"/><hi type="bold">2. Saul tarried in the uttermost part of Gibeah--</hi>Hebrew, "Geba"; entrenched, along with Samuel and Ahiah the high priest, on the top of one of the conical or spherical hills which abound in the Benjamite territory, and favorable for an encampment, called Migron ("a precipice"). <div eID="gen3554" type="x-p"/>
entries.d9d52e1e1598354d96781a07946db757efdb9e61: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv2620"/><div sID="gen3555" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv2620"/><hi type="bold">4. between the passages--</hi>that is, the deep and great ravine of Suweinit.<div eID="gen3555" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3556" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">Jonathan sought to go over unto the Philistines' garrison--</hi>a distance of about three miles running between two jagged points; Hebrew, "teeth of the cliff."<div eID="gen3556" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3557" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">there was a sharp rock on the one side, and a sharp rock on the other side ... Bozez--</hi>("shining") from the aspect of the chalky rock.<div eID="gen3557" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3558" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">Seneh--</hi>("the thorn") probably from a solitary acacia on its top. They are the only rocks of the kind in this vicinity; and the top of the crag towards Michmash was occupied as the post of the Philistines. The two camps were in sight of each other; and it was up the steep rocky sides of this isolated eminence that Jonathan and his armorbearer (<reference osisRef="1Sam.14.6">1Sa 14:6</reference>) made their adventurous approach. This enterprise is one of the most gallant that history or romance records. The action, viewed in itself, was rash and contrary to all established rules of military discipline, which do not permit soldiers to fight or to undertake any enterprise that may involve important consequences without the order of the generals. <div eID="gen3558" type="x-p"/>
entries.8f55f1614d5922ee7a67d6a42fcad955640786a8: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv2621"/><div sID="gen3559" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv2621"/><hi type="bold">6. it may be that the Lord will work for us--</hi>This expression did not imply a doubt; it signified simply that the object he aimed at was not in his own power--but it depended upon God--and that he expected success neither from his own strength nor his own merit. <div eID="gen3559" type="x-p"/>
entries.3ad98a97abc939ca1ea55ac529fa452e4a185169: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv2622"/><div sID="gen3560" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv2622"/><hi type="bold">9-10. if they say, Come up unto us; then we will go up: for the Lord hath delivered them into our hand--</hi>When Jonathan appears here to prescribe a sign or token of God's will, we may infer that the same spirit which inspired this enterprise suggested the means of its execution, and put into his heart what to ask of God. (See on <reference osisRef="Gen.24.12">Ge 24:12</reference>). <div eID="gen3560" type="x-p"/>
entries.e8eba3d137822e24429a3f44970207ce02b018a3: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv2623"/><div sID="gen3561" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv2623"/><hi type="bold">11. Behold, the Hebrews come forth out of the holes--</hi>As it could not occur to the sentries that two men had come with hostile designs, it was a natural conclusion that they were Israelite deserters. And hence no attempt was made to hinder their ascent, or stone them. <div eID="gen3561" type="x-p"/>
entries.11f488905e0f27643bcf9984dcadfd647934f28a: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv2624"/><div sID="gen3562" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv2624"/><hi type="bold">14-15. that first slaughter, which Jonathan and his armour-bearer made, was about twenty men, within as it were an half acre of land, which a yoke of oxen might plow--</hi>This was a very ancient mode of measurement, and it still subsists in the East. The men who saw them scrambling up the rock had been surprised and killed, and the spectacle of twenty corpses would suggest to others that they were attacked by a numerous force. The success of the adventure was aided by a panic that struck the enemy, produced both by the sudden surprise and the shock of an earthquake. The feat was begun and achieved by the faith of Jonathan, and the issue was of God. <div eID="gen3562" type="x-p"/>
entries.be13e23a1615c724bedacc1faf6d955a29a0983a: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv2625"/><div sID="gen3563" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv2625"/><hi type="bold">16. the watchmen of Saul ... looked--</hi>The wild disorder in the enemies' camp was described and the noise of dismay heard on the heights of Gibeah. <div eID="gen3563" type="x-p"/>
entries.2cfe3ae15dab3efdea561caad411aae7d80dde06: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv2626"/><div sID="gen3564" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv2626"/><hi type="bold">17-19. Then said Saul unto the people that were with him, Number now, and see who is gone from us--</hi>The idea occurred to him that it might be some daring adventurer belonging to his own little troop, and it would be easy to discover him. <div eID="gen3564" type="x-p"/>
entries.f03ae35e43be4643d4c4b846f9a2fd4483afc577: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv2629"/><div sID="gen3567" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv2629"/><hi type="bold">20-22. Saul and all the people--</hi>All the warriors in the garrison at Gibeah, the Israelite deserters in the camp of the Philistines, and the fugitives among the mountains of Ephraim, now all rushed to the pursuit, which was hot and sanguinary. <div eID="gen3567" type="x-p"/>
entries.3596d4f1b7d63b2d249154196ba6ef2c64faaa69: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv2630"/><div sID="gen3568" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv2630"/><hi type="bold">23. So the Lord saved Israel that day: and the battle passed over unto Beth-aven--</hi>that is, "Beth-el." It passed over the forest, now destroyed, on the central ridge of Palestine, then over to the other side from the eastern pass of Michmash (<reference osisRef="1Sam.14.31">1Sa 14:31</reference>), to the western pass of Aijalon, through which they escaped into their own plains. <div eID="gen3568" type="x-p"/>
entries.4b6924fae48a82eee0bced5e863b33ebcb6845a4: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv2631"/><div sID="gen3569" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv2631"/><hi type="bold">24. Saul had adjured the people--</hi>Afraid lest so precious an opportunity of effectually humbling the Philistine power might be lost, the impetuous king laid an anathema on any one who should taste food until the evening. This rash and foolish denunciation distressed the people, by preventing them taking such refreshments as they might get on the march, and materially hindered the successful attainment of his own patriotic object. <div eID="gen3569" type="x-p"/>
entries.15b3e4080a8321771bae3ce187f521d4dbf1f1cf: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv2632"/><div sID="gen3570" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv2632"/><hi type="bold">25. all they of the land came to a wood; and there was honey--</hi>The honey is described as "upon the ground," "dropping" from the trees, and in honeycombs--indicating it to be bees' honey. "Bees in the East are not, as in England, kept in hives; they are all in a wild state. The forests literally flow with honey; large combs may be seen hanging on the trees as you pass along, full of honey" [Roberts]. <div eID="gen3570" type="x-p"/>
entries.c6b3e9d2329e61cf2d1960add1d25a29cfc622f9: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv2633"/><div sID="gen3571" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv2633"/><hi type="bold">31-34. the people were very faint. And the people flew upon the spoil--</hi>at evening, when the time fixed by Saul had expired. Faint and famishing, the pursuers fell voraciously upon the cattle they had taken, and threw them on the ground to cut off their flesh and eat them raw, so that the army, by Saul's rashness, were defiled by eating blood, or living animals; probably, as the Abyssinians do, who cut a part of the animal's rump, but close the hide upon it, and nothing mortal follows from that wound. They were painfully conscientious in keeping the king's order for fear of the curse, but had no scruple in transgressing God's command. To prevent this violation of the law, Saul ordered a large stone to be rolled, and those that slaughtered the oxen to cut their throats on that stone. By laying the animal's head on the high stone, the blood oozed out on the ground, and sufficient evidence was afforded that the ox or sheep was dead before it was attempted to eat it. <div eID="gen3571" type="x-p"/>
entries.4ae16151bb3217a26e7da8f2dd09b71ce9a34c63: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv2634"/><div sID="gen3572" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv2634"/><hi type="bold">45. the people rescued Jonathan, that he died not--</hi>When Saul became aware of Jonathan's transgression in regard to the honey, albeit it was done in ignorance and involved no guilt, he was, like Jephthah [Jud 11:31, 35], about to put his son to death, in conformity with his vow [1Sa 14:44]. But the more enlightened conscience of the army prevented the tarnishing the glory of the day by the blood of the young hero, to whose faith and valor it was chiefly due. <div eID="gen3572" type="x-p"/>
entries.e778249ce5f1247d0a6a0c35148a5d3a4eea08a2: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv2635"/><div sID="gen3573" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv2635"/><hi type="bold">47-48. So Saul ... fought against all his enemies on every side--</hi>This signal triumph over the Philistines was followed, not only by their expulsion from the land of Israel, but by successful incursions against various hostile neighbors, whom he harassed though he did not subdue them. <chapter eID="1Sam.14"/>

entries.d1299b465349fc8138c0667abd116db6a8bee693: <div eID="gen10036" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s">Introduction</title> <div sID="gen10037" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen10038" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen10038" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen10037" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen10039" type="x-p"/> Jonathan and his armor-bearer purpose to attack a garrison of the Philistines, <reference osisRef="1Sam.14.1">1Sam 14:1</reference>. Saul and his army, with Ahiah the priest, tarry in Gibeah, <reference osisRef="1Sam.14.2">1Sam 14:2</reference>, <reference osisRef="1Sam.14.3">1Sam 14:3</reference>. Jonathan plans his attack of the Philistine garrison, <reference osisRef="1Sam.14.4-1Sam.14.10">1Sam 14:4-10</reference>. He and his armor-bearer climb over a rock: attack and rout the garrison, <reference osisRef="1Sam.14.11-1Sam.14.15">1Sam 14:11-15</reference>. Saul and has company, seeing confusion on the Philistine host, come out against them; as did the men who had hidden themselves; and the Philistines are defeated, <reference osisRef="1Sam.14.16-1Sam.14.23">1Sam 14:16-23</reference>. Saul lays every man under a curse who shall eat food until the evening; in consequence of which the people are sorely distressed, <reference osisRef="1Sam.14.24-1Sam.14.26">1Sam 14:24-26</reference>. Jonathan, not hearing the adjuration, eats a little honey, which he found on the ground, <reference osisRef="1Sam.14.27-1Sam.14.30">1Sam 14:27-30</reference>. The Philistines being defeated, the people seize on the spoil, and begin to eat flesh without previously bleeding the animals, which Saul endeavors to prevent, <reference osisRef="1Sam.14.31-1Sam.14.34">1Sam 14:31-34</reference>. He builds an altar there, <reference osisRef="1Sam.14.35">1Sam 14:35</reference>. Inquires of the Lord if he may pursue the Philistines by night, but receives no answer, <reference osisRef="1Sam.14.36">1Sam 14:36</reference>, <reference osisRef="1Sam.14.37">1Sam 14:37</reference>. Attributes this to some sin committed by some unknown person: makes inquiry by lot; and finds that Jonathan had tasted the honey, on which he purposes to put him to death, <reference osisRef="1Sam.14.38-1Sam.14.44">1Sam 14:38-44</reference>. The people interpose, and rescue Jonathan, <reference osisRef="1Sam.14.45">1Sam 14:45</reference>. Saul fights against the Moabites, Ammonites, and Amalekites, <reference osisRef="1Sam.14.46-1Sam.14.48">1Sam 14:46-48</reference>. An account of the family of Saul, <reference osisRef="1Sam.14.49-1Sam.14.52">1Sam 14:49-52</reference>. <div eID="gen10039" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10040" type="x-p"/> <hi type="bold">Verse 1</hi> <div eID="gen10040" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10041" type="x-p"/> Come, and let us go over - This action of Jonathan was totally contrary to the laws of war; no military operation should be undertaken without the knowledge and command of the general. But it is likely that he was led to this by a Divine influence. <div eID="gen10041" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10042" type="x-p"/> The armor-bearer is the origin of what we call esquire, from escu, old French, a shield; armiger is the Latin, from arma, weapons, and gero, I bear. In the times of chivalry, the armiger, or esquire, was the servant of the knight who went after him, and carried his lance, shield, etc. It is now (strange to tell!) a title of honor.
entries.fd153d8cf7e72e980ad0d48b3549cb0760eba2c9: <hi type="bold">Verse 2</hi> <div eID="gen10042" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10043" type="x-p"/> Under a pomegranate tree - Under Rimmon, which not only signifies a pomegranate tree, but also a strong rock, in which six hundred Benjamites took shelter, <reference osisRef="Jdg.20.45">Jdg 20:45</reference>. Probably it was in this very rock that Saul and his six hundred men now lay hidden.
entries.7a7003cbe9bf8a58dd95224ca4a42d260e85ab37: <hi type="bold">Verse 3</hi> <div eID="gen10043" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10044" type="x-p"/> Ahiah, the son of Ahitub - Phinehas, son of Eli the high priests had two sons, Ahitub and I-chabod; the latter was born when the ark was taken, and his mother died immediately after. Ahiah is also called Ahimelech, <reference osisRef="1Sam.22.9">1Sam 22:9</reference>. <div eID="gen10044" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10045" type="x-p"/> Wearing an ephod - That is, performing the functions of the high priest. This man does not appear to have been with Saul when he offered the sacrifices, <reference osisRef="1Sam.13.9">1Sam 13:9</reference>, etc.
entries.a6bfde59ff073d958aa8e8379fcb302cd141ce6e: <hi type="bold">Verse 4</hi> <div eID="gen10045" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10046" type="x-p"/> The name of the one was Bozez - Slippery; and the name of the other Seneh, treading down. - Targum.
entries.4854fd218a2cdaa53fa6c9bde52324586d048f39: <hi type="bold">Verse 6</hi> <div eID="gen10046" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10047" type="x-p"/> Let us go over - Moved, doubtless, by a Divine impulse. <div eID="gen10047" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10048" type="x-p"/> There is no restraint to the Lord - This is a fine sentiment; and where there is a promise of defense and support, the weakest, in the face of the strongest enemy, may rely on it with the utmost confidence.
entries.dd01aac83988a87267265270bf05556acb22e0b0: <hi type="bold">Verse 7</hi> <div eID="gen10048" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10049" type="x-p"/> Behold, I am with thee - I shall accompany thee whithersoever thou goest, and share all thy dangers.
entries.c6afb7ad22528ac0e47f68e96665457b15f962b3: <hi type="bold">Verse 9</hi> <div eID="gen10049" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10050" type="x-p"/> If they say thus unto us - Jonathan had no doubt asked this as a sign from God; exactly as Eliezer the servant of Abraham did, <reference osisRef="Gen.24.12">Gen 24:12</reference>.
entries.6de44c615b97b63c070fa19057445e51c5a1987c: <hi type="bold">Verse 12</hi> <div eID="gen10050" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10051" type="x-p"/> Come up to us, and we will show you a thing - This was the favorable sign which Jonathan had requested. The Philistines seem to have meant, Come, and we will show you how well fortified we are, and how able to quell all the attacks of your countrymen.
entries.44d6579f7221e696957989aa5d02e5978ec6afa9: <hi type="bold">Verse 13</hi> <div eID="gen10051" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10052" type="x-p"/> Jonathan climbed up - It seems he had a part of the rock still to get over. When he got over he began to slay the guards, which were about twenty in number, these were of a sort of outpost or advanced guard to the garrison. <div eID="gen10052" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10053" type="x-p"/> Slew after him - Jonathan knocked them down, and the armor-bearer despatched them. This seems to be the meaning.
entries.dda4ba55cae1ee56227c472b9acd14678539358e: <hi type="bold">Verse 14</hi> <div eID="gen10053" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10054" type="x-p"/> A half acre of land - The ancients measured land by the quantum which a yoke of oxen could plough in a day. The original is obscure, and is variously understood. It is probably a proverbial expression for a very small space.
entries.4a3a93189ef87b5b94b9019d7ddae8c839617d99: <hi type="bold">Verse 15</hi> <div eID="gen10054" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10055" type="x-p"/> There was trembling in the host - They were terrified and panic-struck; the people in general round about, those in the garrison, the spoilers, and the whole country, were struck with terror; the commotion was universal and most extraordinary. The trembling of the earth is probably not to be taken literally, but as a metaphor for a great commotion in the country, though God might have interposed in an extraordinary manner, and produced a real earthquake; but their being panic-struck was sufficient to produce all the requisite confusion and dismay.
entries.a519c58fb564887a29a05f0ce358c8cd23a81e37: <hi type="bold">Verse 16</hi> <div eID="gen10055" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10056" type="x-p"/> The watchmen of Saul - Those who were sent out as scouts to observe the motions of the army. <div eID="gen10056" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10057" type="x-p"/> Melted away - There was no order in the Philistine camp, and the people were dispersing in all directions. The Vulgate has, Et ecce multitudo prostrata, "And behold the multitude were prostrate;" many lay dead upon the field, partly by the sword of Jonathan and his armor-bearer, and partly by the swords of each other, <reference osisRef="1Sam.14.20">1Sam 14:20</reference>.
entries.ce0395a5bd49e53eb26dc77ffedba76f182f7a5d: <hi type="bold">Verse 17</hi> <div eID="gen10057" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10058" type="x-p"/> Number now - Saul perceived that the Philistines were routed, but could not tell by what means; supposing that it must be by some of his own troops, he called a muster to see who and how many were absent.
entries.4ded9b9db417e07d56dfcf6368b0443510002c72: <hi type="bold">Verse 18</hi> <div eID="gen10058" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10059" type="x-p"/> Bring hither the ark of God - He wished to inquire what use he should make of the present favorable circumstances, and to proceed in the business as God should direct.
entries.f289dca63c9e2a1d091235e7147af9d509e825df: <hi type="bold">Verse 19</hi> <div eID="gen10059" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10060" type="x-p"/> While Saul talked unto the priest - Before he had made an end of consulting him, the increasing noise of the panic-struck Philistines called his attention; and finding there was no time to lose, he immediately collected his men and fell on them.
entries.48dcba34330b9e7af1f83bcf0adbaf96c634ec12: <hi type="bold">Verse 21</hi> <div eID="gen10060" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10061" type="x-p"/> The Hebrews that were with the Philistines - We may understand such as they held in bondage, or who were their servants. Instead of Hebrews the Septuagint read, οἱ δουλοι, the slaves; from which it is evident that, instead of עברים Ibrim, Hebrews, they found in their text עבדים abadim, servants. But this reading is not countenanced by any other version, nor by any MS. yet discovered.
entries.d89811c7e4617fce5a16f5df38fde5434a91658a: <hi type="bold">Verse 22</hi> <div eID="gen10061" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10062" type="x-p"/> The men - which had hid themselves - See <reference osisRef="1Sam.13.6">1Sam 13:6</reference>. <div eID="gen10062" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10063" type="x-p"/> The Vulgate and the Septuagint add here, And there were with Saul about ten thousand men; but this is supported by no other authority.
entries.f922984f1d3ebec0484963a5ce7035218804cc6d: <hi type="bold">Verse 24</hi> <div eID="gen10063" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10064" type="x-p"/> Saul had adjured the people - He was afraid, if they waited to refresh themselves, the Philistines would escape out of their hands, and therefore he made the taking any food till sunset a capital crime. This was the very means of defeating his own intention; for as the people were exhausted for want of food, they could not continue the pursuit of their enemies: had it not been for this foolish adjuration, there had been a greater slaughter of the Philistines, <reference osisRef="1Sam.14.30">1Sam 14:30</reference>.
entries.d2c9b018b12ac73886b699d771ad67c3a2efdfd3: <hi type="bold">Verse 25</hi> <div eID="gen10064" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10065" type="x-p"/> There was honey upon the ground - There were many wild bees in that country, and Judea is expressly said to be a land flowing with milk and honey.
entries.c59c9b041cebe0a50c1c34e45c8ccd1dae329c98: <hi type="bold">Verse 26</hi> <div eID="gen10065" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10066" type="x-p"/> The honey dropped - It seems to have dropped from the trees on the ground. Honey dews, as they are called, are not uncommon in most countries; and this appears to have been something of this kind. I have seen honey in considerable quantity on the trees and long grass in the fields, and have often eaten of it.
entries.2ea9ad163f3d18788d846ae5cc48eb5556746c10: <hi type="bold">Verse 27</hi> <div eID="gen10066" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10067" type="x-p"/> His eyes were enlightened - Hunger and fatigue affect and dim the sight; on taking food, this affection is immediately removed. This most people know to be a fact.
entries.5a23e9ede48f47c4f56131a4aa45e582049815e6: <hi type="bold">Verse 31</hi> <div eID="gen10067" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10068" type="x-p"/> They smote the Philistines - from Mishmash to Aijalon - The distance Calmet states to be three or four leagues.
entries.a25191184653d69f85f3bb3a35c6b6e618919486: <hi type="bold">Verse 32</hi> <div eID="gen10068" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10069" type="x-p"/> The people did eat them with the blood - They were faint through hunger, and did not take time to bleed the cattle on which they fed. This was another bad effect of Saul's rash adjuration.
entries.8e750900187b4a1cd891cb98c0fc5eeada39bf26: <hi type="bold">Verse 33</hi> <div eID="gen10069" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10070" type="x-p"/> Roll a great stone unto me - Probably this means that they should set up an altar to the Lord, on which the animals might be properly slain, and the blood poured out upon the earth; and a large stone was erected for an altar.
