entries.4cb9d86505edce18b1918f9bd3d17c3334c34d91: <hi type="bold">Verse 35</hi> <div eID="gen10070" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10071" type="x-p"/> Saul built an altar - And this we are informed was the first he had built; Samuel, as prophet had hitherto erected the altars, and Saul thought he had sufficient authority to erect one himself without the prophet, as he once offered sacrifice without him.
entries.062e05321ad4e2ecca7fb6afbfb6236b6b73a79b: <hi type="bold">Verse 36</hi> <div eID="gen10071" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10072" type="x-p"/> Then said the priest - It is evident that Ahiah doubted the propriety of pursuing the Philistines that night; and as a reverse of fortune might be ruinous after such a victory, he wished to have specific directions from the Lord.
entries.a7181716bfb50865ac3bc7ee0e3aa6ee471aead8: <hi type="bold">Verse 37</hi> <div eID="gen10072" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10073" type="x-p"/> He answered him not that day - Why was this answer delayed? Surely Jonathan's eating the honey was no sin. This could not have excited God's displeasure. And yet the lot found out Jonathan! But did this argue that he had incurred guilt in the sight of God? I answer: It did not; for Jonathan was delivered, by the authority of the people, from his father's rash curse; no propitiation is offered for his supposed transgression to induce God to pardon it; nor do we find any displeasure of God manifested on the occasion. See below.
entries.52a4d1e671f46247d0672a9b285618efa883355e: <hi type="bold">Verse 41</hi> <div eID="gen10073" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10074" type="x-p"/> Lord God of Israel, Give a perfect lot - Both the Vulgate and Septuagint add much to this verse: And Saul said to the Lord God of Israel, Lord God of Israel, give judgment. Why is it that thou hast not answered thy servant to-day? If the iniquity be in me, or Jonathan my son, make it manifest. Or if this iniquity be in thy people, give sanctification.
entries.4fde5a0f89ff884bf107161c33bf7b5740ed34e7: <hi type="bold">Verse 42</hi> <div eID="gen10074" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10075" type="x-p"/> And Jonathan was taken - The object of the inquiry most evidently was, "Who has gone contrary to the king's adjuration today?" The answer to that must be Jonathan. But was this a proof of the Divine displeasure against the man? By no means: the holy oracle told the truth, but neither that oracle nor the God who gave it fixed any blame upon Jonathan, and his own conscience acquits him. He seeks not pardon from God, because he is conscious he had not transgressed. But why did not God answer the priest that day? Because he did not think it proper to send the people by night in pursuit of the vanquished Philistines. Saul's motive was perfectly vindictive: Let us go down after the Philistines by night, and spoil them unto the morning light, and let us not leave a man of them; that is, Let us burn, waste, destroy, and slay all before us! Was it right to indulge a disposition of this kind, which would have led to the destruction of many innocent country people, and of many Israelites who resided among the Philistines? Besides, was there not a most manifest reason in the people why God could not be among them? Multitudes of them were defiled in a very solemn manner; they had eaten the flesh with the blood; and however sacrifices might be offered to atone for this transgression of the law, they must continue unclean till the evening. Here were reasons enough why God would not go on with the people for that night.
entries.d119fffd171f537151c74e23bcc6330e614cd13c: <hi type="bold">Verse 44</hi> <div eID="gen10075" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10076" type="x-p"/> And Saul answered - thou shalt surely die, Jonathan - To save thy rash oath! So must John Baptist's head be taken off at the desire of an impure woman, because a Herod had sworn to give her whatever she might request! Unfeeling brute! However, the king was Judge. But what said the people, who were the Jury?
entries.63637517677437542e33aad612bdb0339119a2d3: <hi type="bold">Verse 45</hi> <div eID="gen10076" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10077" type="x-p"/> And the people said - "Shall Jonathan die, who hath wrought this great salvation in Israel? God forbid! As the Lord liveth, there shall not one hair of his head fall to the ground." Here was a righteous and impartial jury, who brought in a verdict according to the evidence: No man should die but for a breach of the law of God; but Jonathan hath not broken any law of God; therefore Jonathan should not die. And because he should not, therefore he shall not. <div eID="gen10077" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10078" type="x-p"/> He hath wrought with God this day - God has been commander-in-chief; Jonathan has acted under his directions. <div eID="gen10078" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10079" type="x-p"/> So the people rescued Jonathan - And God testified no displeasure; and perhaps he permitted all this that he might correct Saul's propensity to rashness and precipitancy.
entries.af8bb852237302ebeab4ee33ab66c85d39d7d9fd: <hi type="bold">Verse 47</hi> <div eID="gen10079" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10080" type="x-p"/> So Saul took the kingdom - The Targum appears to give the meaning of this expression: "Saul prospered in his government over Israel." And the proofs of his prosperity are immediately subjoined. <div eID="gen10080" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10081" type="x-p"/> Fought against all his enemies - Of the wars which are mentioned here we have no particulars; they must have endured a long time, and have been, at least in general, successful.
entries.08d99cb908c244ae78bcfd4cf1be12aa4bb8ecf0: <hi type="bold">Verse 48</hi> <div eID="gen10081" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10082" type="x-p"/> Smote the Amalekites - This war is mentioned in the following chapter.
entries.edd7d927d3ecca8e9605daa3b8fc71dde73e9325: <hi type="bold">Verse 49</hi> <div eID="gen10082" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10083" type="x-p"/> Now the sons of Saul - We do not find Ishbosheth here. Calmet says it was "because he was too young, and did not go with him to the war, for he mentions only those who were with him." Why then mention his daughters and his wife? Did they go with him to the war?
entries.73efe85092c95af089d9df324195cf2f1510f300: <hi type="bold">Verse 52</hi> <div eID="gen10083" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10084" type="x-p"/> When Saul saw any strong man - This was very politic. He thus continued to recruit his army with strong and effective men.  <chapter eID="1Sam.14"/> <div eID="gen10084" type="x-p"/>

entries.0b82e8c10bbd3e9461d53b079019234159d2f5f7: <reference osisRef="1Sam.14.1-1Sam.14.2">1Sa 14:1-2</reference> <div eID="gen3855" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3856" type="x-p"/> Jonathan said to his armour-bearer, “<hi type="italic">We will go over to the post of the Philistines, that is over there</hi>.” To these words, which introduce the occurrences that followed, there are attached from וּלאביו to <reference osisRef="1Sam.14.5">1Sa 14:5</reference> a series of sentences introduced to explain the situation, and the thread of the narrative is resumed in <reference osisRef="1Sam.14.6">1Sa 14:6</reference> by a repetition of Jonathan’s words. It is first of all observed that Jonathan did not disclose his intentions to his father, who would hardly have approved of so daring an enterprise. Then follows a description of the place where Saul was stationed with the six hundred men, viz., “<hi type="italic">at the end of Gibeah</hi> (i.e., the extreme northern end), <hi type="italic">under the pomegranate-tree</hi> (<hi type="italic">Rimmon</hi>) <hi type="italic">which is by Migron</hi>.” <hi type="italic">Rimmon</hi> is not the rock Rimmon (Jdg 20:45), which was on the north-east of Michmash, but is an appellative noun, signifying <hi type="italic">a pomegranate-tree</hi>. <hi type="italic">Migron</hi> is a locality with which we are not acquainted, upon the north side of Gibeah, and a different place from the Migron which was on the north or north-west of Michmash (<reference osisRef="Isa.10.28">Isa 10:28</reference>). <hi type="italic">Gibeah</hi> (<hi type="italic">Tuleil el Phul</hi>) was an hour and a quarter from <hi type="italic">Geba</hi>, and from the pass which led across to Michmash. Consequently, when Saul was encamped with his six hundred men on the north of Gibeah, he may have been hardly an hour’s journey from Geba.
entries.22892c5f3fc61d4566002105d1c736d27b25c0cd: <reference osisRef="1Sam.14.3">1Sa 14:3</reference> <div eID="gen3856" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3857" type="x-p"/> Along with Saul and his six hundred men, there was also <hi type="italic">Ahiah</hi>, the son of Ahitub, the (elder) brother of Ichabod, the son of Phinehas, the son of Eli, the priest at Shiloh, and therefore a great-grandson of Eli, wearing the ephod, i.e., in the high priest’s robes. <hi type="italic">Ahiah</hi> is generally supposed to be the same person as <hi type="italic">Ahimelech</hi>, the son of Ahitub (1Sa 22:9.), in which case <hi type="italic">Ahiah</hi> (אחיּה, brother, i.e., friend of Jehovah) would be only another form of the name Ahimelech (i.e., brother or friend of the King, viz., Jehovah). This is very probable, although Ahimelech might have been Ahaiah’s brother, who succeeded him in the office of high priest on account of his having died without sons, since there is an interval of at least ten years between the events related in this chapter and those referred to in 1 Samuel 22. Ahimelech was afterwards slain by Saul along with the priests of Nob (1Sa 22:9.); the only one who escaped being his son Abiathar, who fled to David and, according to <reference osisRef="1Sam.30.7">1Sa 30:7</reference>, was invested with the ephod. It follows, therefore, that Ahiah (or Ahimelech) must have had a son at least ten years old at the time of the war referred to here, viz., the Abiathar mentioned in <reference osisRef="1Sam.30.7">1Sa 30:7</reference>, and must have been thirty or thirty-five years old himself, since Saul had reigned at least twenty-two years, and Abiathar had become high priest a few years before the death of Saul. These assumptions may be very easily reconciled with the passage before us. As Eli was ninety-eight years old when he died, his son Phinehas, who had been killed in battle a short time before, might have been sixty or sixty-five years old, and have left a son of forty years of age, namely Ahitub. Forty years later, therefore, i.e., at the beginning of Saul’s reign, Ahitub’s son Ahiah (Ahimelech) might have been about fifty years old; and at the death of Ahimelech, which took place ten or twelve years after that, his son Abiathar might have been as much as thirty years of age, and have succeeded his father in the office of high priest. But Abiathar cannot have been older than this when his father died, since he was high priest during the whole of David’s forty years’ reign, until Solomon deposed him soon after he ascended the throne (1Ki 2:26.). Compare with this the remarks on 2Sa 8:17. Jonathan had also refrained from telling the people anything about his intentions, so that they did not know that he had gone.
entries.0257ed65e6d958563578c440c1de910a184e274c: <reference osisRef="1Sam.14.4-1Sam.14.5">1Sa 14:4-5</reference> <div eID="gen3857" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3858" type="x-p"/> In <reference osisRef="1Sam.14.4">1Sa 14:4</reference>, <reference osisRef="1Sam.14.5">1Sa 14:5</reference>, the locality is more minutely described. Between the passes, through which Jonathan endeavoured to cross over to go up to the post of the Philistines, there was a sharp rock on this side, and also one upon the other. One of these was called <hi type="italic">Bozez</hi>, the other <hi type="italic">Seneh</hi>; one (formed) a pillar (מצוּק), i.e., a steep height towards the north opposite to Michmash, the other towards the south opposite to Geba. The expression “<hi type="italic">between the passes</hi>” may be explained from the remark of <hi type="italic">Robinson</hi> quoted above, viz., that at the point where he passed the Wady Suweinit, side wadys enter it from the south-west and north-west. These side wadys supply so many different crossings. Between them, however, on the north and south walls of the deep valley, were the jagged rocks <hi type="italic">Bozez</hi> and <hi type="italic">Seneh</hi>, which rose up like pillars to a great height. These were probably the “hills” which <hi type="italic">Robinson</hi> saw to the left of the pass by which he crossed: “Two hills of a conical or rather spherical form, having steep rocky sides, with small wadys running up behind so as almost to isolate them. One is on the side towards Jeba, and the other towards Mukhmas” (<hi type="italic">Pal</hi>. ii. p. 116).
entries.811a58000cf04d5b27eae8aa925574af9971dabf: <reference osisRef="1Sam.14.6">1Sa 14:6</reference> <div eID="gen3858" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3859" type="x-p"/> And Jonathan said to his armour-bearer, “<hi type="italic">Come, we will go over to the post of these uncircumcised; it may be that Jehovah will work for us; for</hi> (there is) <hi type="italic">no hindrance for Jehovah to work salvation by many or few</hi>.” Jonathan’s resolution arose from the strong conviction that Israel was the nation of God, and possessed in Jehovah an omnipotent God, who would not refuse His help to His people in their conflict with the foes of His kingdom, if they would only put their whole trust in Him.
entries.fe8a78cf17bede2b6ee726345aca4828998df4b3: <reference osisRef="1Sam.14.7">1Sa 14:7</reference> <div eID="gen3859" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3860" type="x-p"/> As the armour-bearer approved of Jonathan’s resolution (לך נטה, <hi type="italic">turn hither</hi>), and was ready to follow him, Jonathan fixed upon a sign by which he would ascertain whether the Lord would prosper his undertaking.
entries.ac545185d6ae3611b30ec9635a9c99fd2b5c5408: <reference osisRef="1Sam.14.8-1Sam.14.10">1Sa 14:8-10</reference> <div eID="gen3860" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3861" type="x-p"/> “<hi type="italic">Behold, we go over to the people and show ourselves to them. If they say to us, Wait</hi> (דּמּוּ, keep quiet) <hi type="italic">till we come to you, we will stand still in our place, and not go up to them; but if they say thus, Come up unto us, then we will go up, for Jehovah hath</hi> (in that case) <hi type="italic">delivered them into our hand</hi>.” The sign was well chosen. If the Philistines said, “Wait till we come,” they would show some courage; but if they said, “Come up to us,” it would be a sign that they were cowardly, and had not courage enough to leave their position and attack the Hebrews. It was not tempting God for Jonathan to fix upon such a sign by which to determine the success of his enterprise; for he did it in the exercise of his calling, when fighting not for personal objects, but for the kingdom of God, which the uncircumcised were threatening to annihilate, and in the most confident belief that the Lord would deliver and preserve His people. Such faith as this God would not put to shame.
entries.3c1768f23b0035f552b0b9a7056f18070788ac46: <reference osisRef="1Sam.14.11-1Sam.14.13">1Sa 14:11-13</reference> <div eID="gen3861" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3862" type="x-p"/> When the two showed themselves to the garrison of the Philistines, they said, “<hi type="italic">Behold, Hebrews come forth out of the holes in which they have hidden themselves</hi>.” And the men of the garrison cried out to Jonathan and his armour-bearer, “<hi type="italic">Come up to us, and we will tell you a word</hi>,” i.e., we will communicate something to you. This was ridicule at the daring of the two men, whilst for all that they had not courage enough to meet them bravely and drive them back. In this Jonathan received the desired sign that the Lord had given the Philistines into the hand of the Israelites: he therefore clambered up the rock on his hands and feet, and his armour-bearer after him; and “<hi type="italic">they</hi> (the Philistines) <hi type="italic">fell before Jonathan</hi>,” i.e., were smitten down by him, “<hi type="italic">and his armour-bearer was slaying behind him</hi>.”
entries.3c8894b7e9a1e89b21aedd24d1f1613af60f8549: <reference osisRef="1Sam.14.14">1Sa 14:14</reference> <div eID="gen3862" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3863" type="x-p"/> The first stroke that Jonathan and his armour-bearer struck was (amounted to) about twenty men “<hi type="italic">on about half a furrow of an acre of field</hi>.” מענה, <hi type="italic">a furrow</hi>, as in <reference osisRef="Ps.129.3">Psa 129:3</reference>, is in the absolute state instead of the construct, because several nouns follow in the construct state (cf. <hi type="italic">Ewald</hi>, §291, <hi type="italic">a</hi>.). צמד, <hi type="italic">lit</hi>. things bound together, then a pair; here it signifies a pair or <hi type="italic">yoke of oxen</hi>, but in the transferred sense of a piece of land that could be ploughed in one morning with a yoke of oxen, like the Latin <hi type="italic">jugum</hi>, <hi type="italic">jugerum</hi>. It is called the furrow of an acre of land, because the <hi type="italic">length</hi> only of half an acre of land was to be given, and not the breadth or the entire circumference. The Philistines, that is to say, took to flight in alarm as soon as the brave heroes really ascended, so that the twenty men were smitten one after another in the distance of half a rood of land. Their terror and flight are perfectly conceivable, if we consider that the outpost of the Philistines was so stationed upon the top of the ridge of the steep mountain wall, that they would not see how many were following, and the Philistines could not imagine it possible that two Hebrews would have ventured to climb the rock alone and make an attack upon them. Sallust relates a similar occurrence in connection with the scaling of a castle in the Numidian war (<hi type="italic">Bell. Jugurth</hi>. c. 89, 90).
entries.b43886bb982c7d95cb1f759a669ab130af158f9a: <reference osisRef="1Sam.14.15">1Sa 14:15</reference> <div eID="gen3863" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3864" type="x-p"/> And there arose a <hi type="italic">terror in the camp upon the field</hi> (i.e., in the principal camp) <hi type="italic">as well as among all the people</hi> (of the advanced outpost of the Philistines); <hi type="italic">the garrison</hi> (i.e., the army that was encamped at Michmash), <hi type="italic">and the spoilers, they also trembled, and the earth quaked</hi>, sc., with the noise and tumult of the frightened foe; “<hi type="italic">and it grew into a trembling of God</hi>,” i.e., a supernatural terror miraculously infused by God into the Philistines. The subject to the last ותּהי is either חרדה, the alarm in the camp, or all that has been mentioned before, i.e., the alarm with the noise and tumult that sprang out of it.<hi type="italic">Flight and defeat of the Philistines</hi>. - 1Sa 14:16. The spies of Saul at Gibeah saw how the multitude (in the camp of the Philistines) melted away and was beaten more and more. The words והלם ויּלך are obscure. The Rabbins are unanimous in adopting the explanation <hi type="italic">magis magisque frangebatur</hi>, and have therefore probably taken הלם as an inf. absol. הלום, and interpreted הלם according to Jdg 5:26. This was also the case with the Chaldee; and <hi type="italic">Gesenius</hi> (<hi type="italic">Thes</hi>. p. 383) has adopted the same rendering, except that he has taken הלם in the sense of <hi type="italic">dissolutus</hi>, <hi type="italic">dissipatus</hi> <hi type="italic">est</hi>. Others take הלום as adverbial (“<hi type="italic">and thither</hi>”), and supply the correlate הלם (hither), so as to bring out the meaning “<hi type="italic">hither and thither</hi>.” Thus the lxx render it ἔνθεν καὶ ἔνθεν, but they have not translated ויּלך at all.
entries.185599fcf846d95e9d62e070da827e82b5159309: <reference osisRef="1Sam.14.17">1Sa 14:17</reference> <div eID="gen3864" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3865" type="x-p"/> Saul conjectured at once that the excitement in the camp of the Philistines was occasioned by an attack made by Israelitish warriors, and therefore commanded the people: פּקדוּ־נא, “<hi type="italic">Muster</hi> (number) <hi type="italic">now, and see who has gone away from us</hi>;” and “<hi type="italic">Jonathan and his armour-bearer were not there</hi>,” i.e., they were missing.
entries.1937224f69e66d63ecc566184ccd2a53eaa377b8: <reference osisRef="1Sam.14.18">1Sa 14:18</reference> <div eID="gen3865" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3866" type="x-p"/> Saul therefore resolved to ask God, through the priest Ahiah, what he should do; whether he should go out with his army against the Philistines or no. But whilst he was talking with the priest, the tumult in the camp of the Philistines became greater and greater, so that he saw from that what ought to be done under the circumstances, and stopped the priest’s inquiring of God, and set out with his people without delay. We are struck, however, with the expression in <reference osisRef="1Sam.14.18">1Sa 14:18</reference>, “<hi type="italic">Bring hither the ark of God</hi>,” and the explanation which follows, “<hi type="italic">for the ark of God was at that time with the children of Israel</hi>,” inasmuch as the ark was then deposited at Kirjath-jearim, and it is a very improbable thing that it should have been in the little camp of Saul. Moreover, in other cases where the high priest is spoken of as inquiring the will of God, there is no mention made of the ark, but only of the ephod, the high priest’s shoulder-dress, upon which there were fastened the Urim and Thummim, through which inquiry was made of God. And in addition to this, the verb הגּישׁה is not really applicable to the ark, which was not an object that could be carried about at will; whereas this verb is the current expression used to signify the fetching of the ephod (vid., <reference osisRef="1Sam.23.9">1Sa 23:9</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Sam.30.7">1Sa 30:7</reference>). All these circumstances render the correctness of the Masoretic text extremely doubtful, notwithstanding the fact that the Chaldee, the Syriac, and Arabic, and the Vulgate support it, and recommend rather the reading adopted by the lxx, προσάγαγε τὸ Ἐφούδ· ὅτι αὐτὸς ἦρεν τὸ Ἐφοὺδ ἐν τῇ ἡμέρᾳ ἐκείνῃ ἐνώπιον Ἰσραήλ, which would give as the Hebrew text, ישׂראל לפני ההוּא בּיּום האפוד נשׂא הוּא כּי האפוד הגּישׁה. In any case, וב'ני ישׂראל@ at the end of the verse should be read ישׂ לבני or לפני, since וּ gives no sense at all.
entries.02d9818a0a6e0295bf8de8cb2a0f839d3163c23d: <reference osisRef="1Sam.14.19">1Sa 14:19</reference> <div eID="gen3866" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3867" type="x-p"/> “<hi type="italic">It increased more and more</hi>;” <hi type="italic">lit</hi>. increasing and becoming greater. The subject וגו וההמון is placed absolutely at the head, so that the verb ויּלך brev eh is appended in the form of an apodosis. ידך אסף, “<hi type="italic">draw thy hand in</hi>” (back); i.e., leave off now.
entries.1aa0ace41bb7c04ebdb99718d6ee3a9aacf7973a: <reference osisRef="1Sam.14.20">1Sa 14:20</reference> <div eID="gen3867" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3868" type="x-p"/> “<hi type="italic">And</hi> (i.e., in consequence of the increasing tumult in the enemy’s camp) <hi type="italic">Saul had himself, and all the people with him, called</hi>,” i.e., called together for battle; and when they came to the war, i.e., to the place of conflict, “<hi type="italic">behold, there was the sword of the one against the other, a very great confusion</hi>,” in consequence partly of terror, and partly of the circumstance alluded to in 1Sa 14:21.
entries.c5f805f8d291b7be36af8d5c9701684128e85f3c: <reference osisRef="1Sam.14.21-1Sam.14.22">1Sa 14:21-22</reference> <div eID="gen3868" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3869" type="x-p"/> “<hi type="italic">And the Hebrews were with the Philistines as before</hi> (yesterday and the day before yesterday), <hi type="italic">who had come along with them in the camp round about; they also came over to Israel, which was with Saul and Jonathan</hi>.” סביב means distributed round about among the Philistines. Those Israelites whom the Philistines had incorporated into their army are called <hi type="italic">Hebrews</hi>, according to the name which was current among foreigners, whilst those who were with Saul are called <hi type="italic">Israel</hi>, according to the sacred name of the nation. The difficulty which many expositors have found in the word להיות has been very correctly solved, so far as the sense is concerned, by the earlier translators, by the interpolation of “<hi type="italic">they returned</hi>:” תבוּ (Chald.), ἐπεστράφησαν (lxx), <hi type="italic">reversi sunt</hi> (<hi type="italic">Vulg.</hi>), and similarly the Syriac and Arabic. We are not at liberty, however, to amend the Hebrew text in this manner, as nothing more is omitted than the finite verb היוּ before the infinitive להיות (for this construction, see <hi type="italic">Gesenius</hi>, <hi type="italic">Gramm</hi>. §132, 3, Anm. 1), and this might easily be left out here, since it stands at the beginning of the verse in the main clause. The literal rendering would be, they were to be with Israel, i.e., they came over to Israel. The fact that the Hebrews who were serving in the army of the Philistines came over to Saul and his host, and turned their weapons against their oppressors, naturally heightened the confusion in the camp of the Philistines, and accelerated their defeat; and this was still further increased by the fact that the Israelites who had concealed themselves on the mountains of Ephraim also joined the Israelitish army, as soon as they heard of the flight of the Philistines (<reference osisRef="1Sam.14.22">1Sa 14:22</reference>).
entries.e601cf3fb5016c1deb838f900c42608c9bd91f47: <reference osisRef="1Sam.14.23">1Sa 14:23</reference> <div eID="gen3869" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3870" type="x-p"/> “<hi type="italic">Thus the Lord helped Israel that day, and the conflict went out beyond Bethaven</hi>.” <hi type="italic">Bethaven</hi> was on the east of Michmash, and, according to <reference osisRef="1Sam.14.31">1Sa 14:31</reference>, the Philistines fled westwards from Michmash to Ajalon. But if we bear in mind that the camp of the Philistines was on the eastern side of Michmash before Bethaven, according to <reference osisRef="1Sam.13.5">1Sa 13:5</reference>, and that the Israelites forced their way into it from the south, we shall see that the battle might easily have spread out beyond Bethaven, and that eventually the main body of the enemy might have fled as far as Ajalon, and have been pursued to that point by the victorious Israelites.<hi type="italic">Saul’s precipitate haste</hi>. - 1Sa 14:24. The men of Israel <hi type="italic">were pressed</hi> (i.e., fatigued) <hi type="italic">on that day</hi>, sc., through the military service and fighting. Then Saul adjured the people, saying, “<hi type="italic">Cursed be the man that eateth bread until the evening, and</hi> (till) <hi type="italic">I have avenged myself upon mine enemies</hi>.” יאל, <hi type="italic">fut. apoc</hi>. of יאלה for יאלה, from אלה, to swear, <hi type="italic">Hiphil</hi> to adjure or require an oath of a person. The people took the oath by saying “<hi type="italic">amen</hi>” to what Saul had uttered. This command of Saul did not proceed from a proper attitude towards the Lord, but was an act of false zeal, in which Saul had more regard to himself and his own kingly power than to the cause of the kingdom of Jehovah, as we may see at once from the expression וגו נקּמתּי, “till <hi type="italic">I</hi> have avenged <hi type="italic">myself</hi> upon mine enemies.” It was a despotic measure which not only failed to accomplish its object (see <reference osisRef="1Sam.14.30">1Sa 14:30</reference>, <reference osisRef="1Sam.14.31">1Sa 14:31</reference>), but brought Saul into the unfortunate position of being unable to carry out the oath (see <reference osisRef="1Sam.14.45">1Sa 14:45</reference>). All the people kept the command. “<hi type="italic">They tasted no bread</hi>.” ולא־טעם is not to be connected with ונקּמתּי as an apodosis.
entries.8c6a019de8eedcdc55862e07fe6d6a2f996fabaf: <reference osisRef="1Sam.14.25">1Sa 14:25</reference> <div eID="gen3870" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3871" type="x-p"/> “<hi type="italic">And all the land</hi> (i.e., all the people of the land who had gathered round Saul: vid., <reference osisRef="1Sam.14.29">1Sa 14:29</reference>) <hi type="italic">came into the woody country; there was honey upon the field</hi>.” יער signifies here a woody district, in which forests alternated with tracts of arable land and meadows.
entries.67b1f48218d92278187160afa83b3c4d9d3ce64f: <reference osisRef="1Sam.14.26">1Sa 14:26</reference> <div eID="gen3871" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3872" type="x-p"/> When the people came into the wood and saw <hi type="italic">a stream of honey</hi> (or wild or wood bees), “<hi type="italic">no one put his hand to his mouth</hi> (sc., to eat of the honey), <hi type="italic">because they feared the oath</hi>.”
entries.0ce9d2a5deecfeca66faf48e00483c6555edcbb6: <reference osisRef="1Sam.14.27">1Sa 14:27</reference> <div eID="gen3872" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3873" type="x-p"/> But Jonathan, who had not heard his father’s oath, dipped (in the heat of pursuit, that he might not have to stop) the point of his staff in the new honey, and put it to his mouth, “<hi type="italic">and his eyes became bright</hi>;” his lost strength, which is reflected in the eye, having been brought back by this invigorating taste. The <hi type="italic">Chethibh</hi> תראנה is probably to be read תּראנה, the eyes became seeing, received their power of vision again. The Masoretes have substituted as the <hi type="italic">Keri</hi> תּארנה, from אור, to become bright, according to <reference osisRef="1Sam.14.29">1Sa 14:29</reference>; and this is probably the correct reading, as the letters might easily be transposed.
entries.1cc59e0c1887ea890b0bef8f9d045f7273ab2854: <reference osisRef="1Sam.14.28-1Sam.14.30">1Sa 14:28-30</reference> <div eID="gen3873" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3874" type="x-p"/> When one of the people told him thereupon of his father’s oath, in consequence of which the people were exhausted (העם ויּעף belongs to the man’s words; and ויּעף is the same as in Jdg 4:21), Jonathan condemned the prohibition. “<hi type="italic">My father has brought the land</hi> (i.e., the people of the land, as in <reference osisRef="1Sam.14.25">1Sa 14:25</reference>) <hi type="italic">into trouble</hi> (עכר, see at <reference osisRef="Gen.34.30">Gen 34:30</reference>): <hi type="italic">see how bright mine eyes have become because I tasted a little of this honey. How much more if the people had eaten to-day of the booty of its enemies, would not the overthrow among the Philistines truly have then become great?</hi>” כּי אף, lit. to this (there comes) also that = not to mention how much more; and עתּה כּי is an emphatic introduction of the apodosis, as in <reference osisRef="Gen.31.42">Gen 31:42</reference>; <reference osisRef="Gen.43.10">Gen 43:10</reference>, and other passages, and the apodosis itself is to be taken as a question.<hi type="italic">Result of the battle, and consequences of Saul’s rashness</hi>. - 1Sa 14:31. “<hi type="italic">On that day they smote the Philistines from Michmash to Ajalon</hi>,” which has been preserved in the village of <hi type="italic">Yâlo</hi> (see at <reference osisRef="Josh.19.42">Jos 19:42</reference>), and was about three geographical miles to the south-west of Michmash; “<hi type="italic">and the people were very faint</hi>,” because Saul had forbidden them to eat before the evening (<reference osisRef="1Sam.14.24">1Sa 14:24</reference>).
entries.46b6cf96fc7c2f6d6c434ba77f600884171cc140: <reference osisRef="1Sam.14.32">1Sa 14:32</reference> <div eID="gen3874" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3875" type="x-p"/> They therefore “<hi type="italic">fell voraciously upon the booty</hi>” - (the <hi type="italic">Chethibh</hi> ויּעשׂ is no doubt merely an error in writing for ויּעט, <hi type="italic">imperf</hi>. <hi type="italic">Kal</hi> of עיט with <hi type="italic">Dagesh forte implic</hi>. instead of ויּעט, as we may see from <reference osisRef="1Sam.15.19">1Sa 15:19</reference>, since the meaning required by the context, viz., to fall upon a thing, cannot be established in the case of עשׂה with על. On the other hand, there does not appear to be any necessity to supply the article before שׁלל, and this <hi type="italic">Keri</hi> seems only to have been taken from the parallel passage in <reference osisRef="1Sam.15.19">1Sa 15:19</reference>), - “<hi type="italic">and took sheep, and oxen, and calves, and slew them on the ground</hi> (ארצה, <hi type="italic">lit</hi>. to the earth, so that when they were slaughtered the animal fell upon the ground, and remained lying in its blood, and was cut in pieces), <hi type="italic">and ate upon the blood</hi>” (הדּם על, with which הדּם אל, “<hi type="italic">lying to the blood</hi>,” is interchanged in <reference osisRef="1Sam.14.34">1Sa 14:34</reference>), i.e., the flesh along with the blood which adhered to it, by doing which they sinned against the law in Lev 19:26. This sin had been occasioned by Saul himself through the prohibition which he issued.
entries.0bd0a118aae4442d49f0aef0946b13d6a149dfec: <reference osisRef="1Sam.14.33-1Sam.14.34">1Sa 14:33-34</reference> <div eID="gen3875" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3876" type="x-p"/> When this was told to Saul, he said, “<hi type="italic">Ye act faithlessly towards Jehovah</hi>” by transgressing the laws of the covenant; “<hi type="italic">roll me now</hi> (lit. this day) <hi type="italic">a large stone. Scatter yourselves among the people, and say to them, Let every one bring his ox and his sheep to me, and slay here</hi>” (upon the stone that has been rolled up), viz., so that the blood could run off properly upon the ground, and the flesh be separated from the blood. This the people also did.
entries.3d0f870b87748930bf19f08c9967fe9d912e2d9e: <reference osisRef="1Sam.14.35">1Sa 14:35</reference> <div eID="gen3876" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3877" type="x-p"/> As a thanksgiving for this victory, Saul built an altar to the Lord. לבנות החל אתו, “<hi type="italic">he began to build it</hi>,” i.e., he built this altar at the beginning, or as the first altar. This altar was probably not intended to serve as a place of sacrifice, but simply to be a memorial of the presence of God, or the revelation of God which Saul had received in the marvellous victory.
entries.052bbf89ddc774b0adbeb33ab0f5dbd56726ce65: <reference osisRef="1Sam.14.36">1Sa 14:36</reference> <div eID="gen3877" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3878" type="x-p"/> After the people had strengthened themselves in the evening with food, Saul wanted to pursue the Philistines still farther during the night, and to plunder among them until the light (i.e., till break of day), and utterly destroy them. The people assented to this proposal, but the priest (Ahiah) wished first of all to obtain the decision of God upon the matter. “<hi type="italic">We will draw near to God here</hi>” (before the altar which has just been built).
entries.c6b0ebab27033371fb339396a83079b12638c495: <reference osisRef="1Sam.14.37">1Sa 14:37</reference> <div eID="gen3878" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3879" type="x-p"/> But when Saul inquired of God (through the Urim and Thummim of the high priest), “<hi type="italic">Shall I go down after the Philistines? wilt Thou deliver them into the hand of Israel?</hi>” God did not answer him. Saul was to perceive from this, that the guilt of some sin was resting upon the people, on account of which the Lord had turned away His countenance, and was withdrawing His help.
entries.6ab634f15b0369b3fed6907d9d3936eebb0d9e18: <reference osisRef="1Sam.14.38-1Sam.14.39">1Sa 14:38-39</reference> <div eID="gen3879" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3880" type="x-p"/> When Saul perceived, this, he directed all the heads of the people (<hi type="italic">pinnoth</hi>, as in Jdg 20:2) to draw near to learn whereby (wherein) the sin had occurred that day, and declared, “<hi type="italic">As truly as Jehovah liveth, who has brought salvation to Israel, even if it were upon Jonathan my son, he shall die</hi>.” The first כּי in <reference osisRef="1Sam.14.39">1Sa 14:39</reference> is explanatory; the second and third serve to introduce the words, like ὅτι, <hi type="italic">quod</hi>; and the repetition serves to give emphasis, lit., “<hi type="italic">that even if it were upon my son, that he shall die</hi>.” “<hi type="italic">And of all the people no one answered him</hi>,” from terror at the king’s word.
entries.82ed7c956f7d8cc60bfa349c74d7c453ce9ece19: <reference osisRef="1Sam.14.40-1Sam.14.41">1Sa 14:40-41</reference> <div eID="gen3880" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3881" type="x-p"/> In order to find out the guilt, or rather the culprit, Saul proceeded to the lot; and for this purpose he made all the people stand on one side, whilst he and his son Jonathan went to the other, and then solemnly addressed Jehovah thus: “<hi type="italic">God of Israel, give innocence</hi> (of mind, i.e., truth). <hi type="italic">And the lot fell upon Saul and Jonathan</hi> (ילּכד, as in <reference osisRef="1Sam.10.20-1Sam.10.21">1Sa 10:20-21</reference>); <hi type="italic">and the people went out</hi>,” sc., without the lot falling upon them, i.e., they went out free.
entries.286e5e12dfa3bc822fb1f21aaa9cfc12149f6253: <reference osisRef="1Sam.14.42">1Sa 14:42</reference> <div eID="gen3881" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3882" type="x-p"/> When they proceeded still further to cast lots between Saul and his son (הפּילוּ, sc., גּורל; cf. <reference osisRef="1Chr.26.14">1Ch 26:14</reference>; <reference osisRef="Neh.11.11">Neh 11:11</reference>, etc.), <hi type="italic">Jonathan was taken</hi>.<note placement="foot">In the Alex. version, vv. 41 and 42 are lengthened out with long paraphrases upon the course pursued in casting the lots: καὶ εἶπε Σαούλ, Κύριε ὁ θεὸς Ἰσραήλ τί ὅτι οὐκ ἀπεκρίθης τῷ δούλῳ σου σήμερον; ει ̓ ἐν ἐμοὶ ἢ ἐν Ἰωνάθαν τῷ υἱῷ μου ἡ ἀδικία; κύριε ὁ θεὸς Ἰσραήλ δὸς δήλους· καὶ ἐἀν τάδε εἴπῃ δὸς δὴ τῷ λαῷ σου Ἰσραήλ, δός δὴ ὁσιότηατ, καὶ κληροῦται Ἰωνάθαν καὶ Σαούλ καὶ ὁ λαὸς ἐξῆλθε. V. 42: Καὶ εἶπε Σαοὑλ, βάλλετε ἀνὰ μέσον ἐμοῦ καὶ ἀνὰ μέσον Ἰωνάθαν τοῦ υἱοῦ μου· ὃν ἂν κατακληρώσηται Κύριος ἀποθανέτω. Καὶ εἶπεν ὁ λαὸς πρὸς Σαούλ, οὐκ ἔστι τὸ ῥῆμα τοῦτο. Καὶ κατεκράτησε Σαοὺλ τοῦ λαοῦ, καὶ βάλλουσιν ἀνὰ μέσον αὐτοῦ καὶ ἀνὰ μέσον Ἰωνάθαν τοῦ υἱοῦ αὐτοῦ, καὶ κατακληροῦται Ἰωναθαν. One portion of these additions is also found in the text of our present Vulgate, and reads as follows: <hi type="italic">Et dixit Saul ad Dominum Deum Israel: Domine Deus Israel, da indicium! quid est quod non responderis servo tuo hodie? Si in me aut in Jonathan filio meo est iniquitas, da ostensionem; aut si haec iniquitas est in populo tuo, da sanctitatem. Et deprehensus est Jonathas et Saul, populus autem exivit.</hi> The beginning and end of this verse, as well as v. 42, agree here most accurately with the Hebrew text. But the words from <hi type="italic">quid est quod </hi>to<hi type="italic">da sanctitatem</hi> are interpolated, so that תמים הבה are translated twice; first in the words <hi type="italic">da indicium</hi>, and then in the interpolation <hi type="italic">da ostensionem</hi>. This repetition of the same words, and that in different renderings, when taken in connection with the agreement of the Vulgate with the Hebrew text at the beginning and end of the verse, shows clearly enough, that the interpolated clauses did not originate with <hi type="italic">Jerome</hi>, but are simply inserted in his translation from the Itala. The additions of the lxx, in which τάδε εἶπῃ is evidently only a distortion of ἡ ἀδικία, are regarded by <hi type="italic">Ewald</hi> (<hi type="italic">Gesch. </hi>iii. p. 48) and Thenius as an original portion of the text which has dropped out from the Masoretic text. They therefore infer, that instead of תמים we ought to read תּמּים (<hi type="italic">Thummim</hi>), and that we have here the full formula used in connection with the use of the Urim and Thummim, from which it may be seen, that this mode of divine revelation consisted simply in a sacred lot, or in the use of two dice, the one of which was fixed upon at the outset as meaning <hi type="italic">no</hi>, and the other as meaning <hi type="italic">yes</hi>. So much at any rate is indisputable, that the Septuagint translator took תמים in the sense of <hi type="italic">thummim</hi>, and so assumed that Saul had the guilty person discovered by resorting to the Urim and Thummim. But this assumption is also decidedly erroneous, together with all the inferences based upon it. For, in the first place, the verbs הפּיל and ילּכד can be proved to be never used throughout the whole of the Old Testament to signify the use of the Urim and Thummim, and to be nothing more than technical expressions used to denote the casting of a simple lot (see the passages cited above in the text). Moreover, such passages as <reference osisRef="1Sam.10.22">1Sa 10:22</reference>, and <reference osisRef="1Sam.2.5">1Sa 2:5</reference>, <reference osisRef="1Sam.2.23">1Sa 2:23</reference>, show most unmistakeably that the divine oracle of the Urim and Thummim did not consist merely in a sacred lot with yes and no, but that God gave such answers through it as could never have been given through the lots. The Septuagint expansions of the text are nothing more, therefore, than a subjective and really erroneous interpretation on the part of the translators, which arose simply from the mistaken idea that תמים was <hi type="italic">thummim</hi>, and which is therefore utterly worthless.</note>
entries.62185c3acc86b3245d4acdd4bb9956667c465040: <reference osisRef="1Sam.14.43-1Sam.14.44">1Sa 14:43-44</reference> <div eID="gen3882" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3883" type="x-p"/> When Saul asked him what he had done, Jonathan confessed that he had tasted a little honey (see <reference osisRef="1Sam.14.27">1Sa 14:27</reference>), and resigned himself to the punishment suspended over him, saying, “<hi type="italic">Behold, I shall die</hi>;” and Saul pronounced sentence of death upon him, accompanying it with an oath (“<hi type="italic">God do so</hi>,” etc.: vid., Rth 1:17).
entries.c79cb78aa36d1b2c8ae1928b39d48af68ddf6cc2: <reference osisRef="1Sam.14.45">1Sa 14:45</reference> <div eID="gen3883" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3884" type="x-p"/> But the people interposed, “<hi type="italic">Shall Jonathan die, who has achieved this great salvation</hi> (victory) <hi type="italic">in Israel? God forbid! As truly as Jehovah liveth, not a hair shall fall from his head upon the ground; for he hath wrought</hi> (the victory) <hi type="italic">with God to-day</hi>.” Thus the people delivered Jonathan from death. The objection raised by the people was so conclusive, that Saul was obliged to yield. <div eID="gen3884" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3885" type="x-p"/> What Jonathan had done was not wrong in itself, but became so simply on account of the oath with which Saul had forbidden it. But Jonathan did not hear the oath, and therefore had not even consciously transgressed. Nevertheless a curse lay upon Israel, which was to be brought to light as a warning for the culprit. Therefore Jehovah had given no reply to Saul. But when the lot, which had the force of a divine verdict, fell upon Jonathan, sentence of death was not thereby pronounced upon him by God; but is was simply made manifest, that through his transgression of his father’s oath, with which he was not acquainted, guilt had been brought upon Israel. The breach of a command issued with a solemn oath, even when it took place unconsciously, excited the wrath of God, as being a profanation of the divine name. But such a sin could only rest as guilt upon the man who had committed, or the man who occasioned it. Now where the command in question was one of God himself, there could be no question, that even in the case of unconscious transgression the sin fell upon the transgressor, and it was necessary that it should either be expiated by him or forgiven him. But where the command of a man had been unconsciously transgressed, the guilt might also fall upon the man who issued the command, that is to say, if he did it without being authorized or empowered by God. In the present instance, Saul had issued the prohibition without divine authority, and had made it obligatory upon the people by a solemn oath. The people had conscientiously obeyed the command, but Jonathan had transgressed it without being aware of it. For this Saul was about to punish him with death, in order to keep his oath. But the people opposed it. They not only pronounced Jonathan innocent, because he had broken the king’s command unconsciously, but they also exclaimed that he had gained the victory for Israel “<hi type="italic">with God</hi>.” In this fact (Jonathan’s victory) there was a divine verdict. And Saul could not fail to recognise now, that it was not Jonathan, but he himself, who had sinned, and through his arbitrary and despotic command had brought guilt upon Israel, on account of which God had given him no reply.
entries.6aaaea7abd1bcb7f3f4708707ae9c63d81ef4a88: <reference osisRef="1Sam.14.46">1Sa 14:46</reference> <div eID="gen3885" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3886" type="x-p"/> With the feeling of this guilt, Saul gave up any further pursuit of the Philistines: he “<hi type="italic">went up</hi>” (sc., to Gibeah) “<hi type="italic">from behind the Philistines</hi>,” i.e., desisting from any further pursuit. But the Philistines went to their place, i.e., back into their own land.
entries.68ca6223ddbf6a8cb3b2e2301a9a7d5f84ad35ed: <reference osisRef="1Sam.14.47-1Sam.14.52">1Sa 14:47-52</reference> <div eID="gen3886" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3887" type="x-p"/> General Summary of Saul’s other Wars, and Account of his Family. - 1Sa 14:47. “<hi type="italic">But Saul had taken the sovereignty</hi>.” As Saul had first of all secured a recognition of himself as king on the part of all the tribes of Israel, through his victory over the Ammonites at Jabesh (1Sa 11:12.), so it was through the victory which he had gained over the Philistines, and by which these obstinate foes of Israel were driven back into their own land, that he first acquired the kingship over Israel, i.e., first really secured the regal authority over the Israelites. This is the meaning of המּלוּכה לכד; and this statement is not at variance either with the election of Saul by lot (1Sa 10:17.), or with his confirmation at Gilgal (<reference osisRef="1Sam.11.14-1Sam.11.15">1Sa 11:14-15</reference>). But as Saul had to fight for the sovereignty, and could only secure it by successful warfare, his other wars are placed in the foreground in the summary account of his reign which follows (<reference osisRef="1Sam.14.47">1Sa 14:47</reference>, <reference osisRef="1Sam.14.48">1Sa 14:48</reference>), whilst the notices concerning his family, which stand at the very beginning in the case of other kings, are not mentioned till afterwards (<reference osisRef="1Sam.14.49-1Sam.14.51">1Sa 14:49-51</reference>). Saul fought successfully against all the enemies of Israel round about; against Moab, the Ammonites, Edom, the kings of Zobah, a district of Syria on this side the Euphrates (see at <reference osisRef="2Sam.8.3">2Sa 8:3</reference>), and against the Philistines. The war against the Ammonites is described in <reference osisRef="1Sam.11.1-1Sam.11.15">1Sa 11:1-15</reference>; but with the Philistines Saul had to wage repeated war all the days of his life (<reference osisRef="1Sam.14.52">1Sa 14:52</reference>). The other wars are none of them more fully described, simply because they were of no importance to the history of the kingdom of God, having neither furnished occasion for any miraculous displays of divine omnipotence, nor brought about the subjection of hostile nations to the power of Israel. “<hi type="italic">Whithersoever he turned, he inflicted punishment</hi>.” This is the rendering which Luther has very aptly given to ירשׁיא; for הרשׁיע signifies to declare wrong, hence to condemn, more especially as applied to judges: here it denotes sentence or condemnation <hi type="italic">by deeds</hi>. Saul chastised these nations for their attacks upon Israel.

Nor was it necessary he should inform him of it, because he had a Commission from his Father, to Fight when he saw occasion; as he had done without his Fathers privity, <ns0:hi>Chap.</ns0:hi> 13. 3.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>

                  <ns0:p n="6">6 And Jonathan said to the young man that bare his armour, Come, and let us go over unto the garison of these uncircumcised <ns0:note n="k" place="bottom">So he calls them, partly in contempt, and principally to strengthen his Faith by this consideration, That his Enemies were Enemies to God, and without any hope in God, or help from him; whereas he was Circumcised, and therefore in Covenant with God, who was both able, and engaged to assist his people.</ns0:note>, it may be <ns0:note n="l" place="bottom">He speaks doubtfully: for though he found and felt himself stirred up by God to this Exploit, and was assured that God would deliver his People; yet he was not certain that he would do it at this time, and in this way.</ns0:note> that the LORD will work <ns0:note n="m" place="bottom">To wit, great and wonderful things.</ns0:note> for us: for <ns0:hi>there is</ns0:hi> no re<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />straint to the LORD <ns0:note n="n" place="bottom">There is no per<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />son nor thing which can hinder God from thus doing.</ns0:note>

                  <ns0:p n="7">7 And his armour-bearer said unto him, Do all that <ns0:hi>is</ns0:hi> in thine heart: turn thee <ns0:note n="o" place="bottom">March on to the Enemies.</ns0:note>: behold, I <ns0:hi>am</ns0:hi> with thee according to thy heart.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="8">
                     <ns0:pb facs="tcp:107763:228" />8 Then said Jonathan, Behold, we will pass over unto <ns0:hi>these</ns0:hi> men, and we will discover our selves unto them.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="9">9 If they say thus unto us, <ns0:note n="†" place="margin">
                        <ns0:hi>Heb.</ns0:hi> be still.</ns0:note> Tarry until we come to you: then we will stand still in our place, and will not go up unto them.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="10">10 But if they say thus, Come up unto us: then we will go up: for the LORD hath delivered them into our hand: and this <ns0:hi>shall be</ns0:hi> a sign unto us <ns0:note n="p" place="bottom">
                        <ns0:hi>Ionathan</ns0:hi> not being assured of the success of this pre<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />sent Exploit, desires a sign; and, by the instinct of God's Spirit, as the success shews, pitcheth upon this. Divers such heroical Motions and extraordinary impulses there were among great and good men in ancient times; as <ns0:hi>Gen.</ns0:hi> 24. 13. <ns0:hi>Iudg.</ns0:hi> 6. 37. which are not presidents to us.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="11">11 And both of them discovered themselves un<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />to the garison of the Philistines: and the Philistines said, Behold, the Hebrews come forth out of the holes <ns0:note n="q" place="bottom">Therefore <ns0:hi>Ionathan</ns0:hi> chose that Rocky and unusual way, that the <ns0:hi>Philistines</ns0:hi> might suppose they did not come from <ns0:hi>Saul</ns0:hi>'s Camp to Fight with them, but rather out of the Caves, and holes of the Rocks, from which their necessity had now driven them.</ns0:note>, where they had hid themselves.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="12">12 And the men of the garison answered Jo<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />nathan and his armour-bearer, and said, Come up to us, and we will shew you a thing <ns0:note n="r" place="bottom">We having something of Importance to communicate to you. A Speech of contempt and derision.</ns0:note>. And Jona<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />than said unto his armour-bearer, Come up after me, for the Lord hath delivered them <ns0:note n="s" place="bottom">He piously and modestly ascribes the Success which he now foresees, to God onely.</ns0:note> into the hand of Israel.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="13">13 And Jonathan climbed up upon his hands, and upon his feet, and his armour-bearer after him <ns0:note n="t" place="bottom">The <ns0:hi>Philistines</ns0:hi> could easily have hindred their Ascent, but thought scorn to do it, not questioning but they could cut them off in a moment when they were come up to them according to their invitation.</ns0:note>: and they fell before Jonathan, and his armour<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />bearer slew after him <ns0:note n="u" place="bottom">For being endowed with extraordinary strength and courage, and having with incre<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />dible boldness killed the first they met with, and so pro<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ceeding with success, it is not strange if the <ns0:hi>Philistines</ns0:hi> were both astonished and intimidated; God also struck them with a Panick Terror; and withal, infatuated their Minds, and possibly, put an Evil Spirit among them, which in this uni<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />versal Confusion made them conceive that there was Trea<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />chery amongst themselves, and therefore caused them to sheath their Swords in one anothers Bowels; as appears from <ns0:hi>v.</ns0:hi> 16, 20.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="14">14 And that first slaughter which Jonathan and his armour-bearer made, was about twenty men, within as it were <ns0:note n="‖" place="margin">
                        <ns0:hi>Or,</ns0:hi> half a fur<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />row of an acre of land.</ns0:note> an half acre of land; <ns0:hi>which</ns0:hi> a yoke <ns0:hi>of oxen might plow.</ns0:hi>
                  </ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="15">15 And there was trembling <ns0:note n="x" place="bottom">A great Consternation; partly, from this unexpected and prodigious Slaughter, which made them suspect, there was more than Man in the Case; and that the Lord (of whose infinite Power they had had former experience) was come forth to Fight against them; and partly, from the Lord, who took away their Spirits and Strength, and struck them with Fear and Amazement.</ns0:note> in the host, in the field <ns0:note n="y" place="bottom">
                        <ns0:hi>i. e.</ns0:hi> In the whole Host which was there in the Field.</ns0:note>, and among all the people <ns0:note n="z" place="bottom">
                        <ns0:hi>i. e.</ns0:hi> Among all the rest of their For<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ces, as well those in the Garison, (as it is here explained in the following words) at <ns0:hi>Michmash,</ns0:hi> as the Spoilers, mentio<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ned <ns0:hi>chap.</ns0:hi> 13. 17. the report of this Prodigy, and with it the Terror of God speedily passing from one to another.</ns0:note>: the gari<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />son, and the spoilers, they also trembled, and the earth quaked <ns0:note n="a" place="bottom">Either 1. Metaphorically and Hyperbolically, the whole Land; <ns0:hi>i. e.</ns0:hi> the Inhabitants of the Land: to wit, of the <ns0:hi>Philistines,</ns0:hi> Trembled. Or rather, 2.                         <ns0:hi>i. e.</ns0:hi> were strangely and suddenly dispersed, and put to Flight.</ns0:note>, and they went on beating down <ns0:hi>one another</ns0:hi> 
                     <ns0:note n="e" place="bottom">Ei<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ther, 1. accidentally through hasty Flight: Or 2. with De<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />sign to destroy one another as the Authors or Abettors of the present Calamity.                   <ns0:p n="17">17 Then said Saul unto the people that <ns0:hi>were</ns0:hi> with him, Number now, and see who is gone from us <ns0:note n="f" place="bottom">For he probably supposed, that not onely <ns0:hi>Ionathan,</ns0:hi> but also some considerable number of his Army <ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#APEX" extent="1 word">
                           <ns0:desc>〈◊〉</ns0:desc>
                        </ns0:gap>, and that by them that Slaughter was made.</ns0:note>. And when they had numbred, behold Jona<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />than and his armour-bearer <ns0:hi>were</ns0:hi> not <ns0:hi>there.</ns0:hi>
                  </ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="18">18 And Saul said unto Ahiah, Bring hither the ark of God <ns0:note n="g" place="bottom">That the Priest may put on the Ephod, and may en<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />quire of the Lord before the Ark what the occasion of this Tumult among our Enemies is, and what we shall do.</ns0:note>: (for the ark of God was at that time with the children of Israel <ns0:note n="h" place="bottom">To wit, in the Camp, whither sometimes it was brought; as 1 <ns0:hi>Sam.</ns0:hi> 4. 5. And now the rather, partly because it was now in an unsetled condition, and without the Tabernacle, and therefore easily removed from place to place: and partly, because <ns0:hi>Saul</ns0:hi> thought to compensate <ns0:hi>Samuel</ns0:hi>'s absence with the presence of the Ark.</ns0:note>.)</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="19">19 ¶ And it came to pass while Saul talked unto the priest, that the <ns0:note n="‖" place="margin">
                        <ns0:hi>Or.</ns0:hi>

                  <ns0:p n="21">21 Moreover, the Hebrews <ns0:hi>that</ns0:hi> were with the Philistines before that time, which went up with them into the camp <ns0:note n="l" place="bottom">Either by constraint, as Servants; or in Policy, to gain their favour and protection.</ns0:note>, <ns0:hi>from the countrey</ns0:hi> round about, even they also <ns0:hi>turned</ns0:hi> to be with the Israelites that were with Saul and Jonathan.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="22">22 Likewise all the men of Israel, which <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Chap. 13 6.</ns0:note> had hid themselves in mount Ephraim, <ns0:hi>when</ns0:hi> they heard that the Philistines fled, even they also followed hard after them in the battel.</ns0:p>

Cursed <ns0:hi>be</ns0:hi> the man that eateth <ns0:hi>any</ns0:hi> food until even<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ing, that I may be avenged on mine enemies <ns0:note n="o" place="bottom">As <ns0:hi>Sauls</ns0:hi> in<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#APEX" extent="1+ letters">
                           <ns0:desc>•…</ns0:desc>
                        </ns0:gap>mion was good; namely, to Execute Ven<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />geance upon Gods and his Enemies: so the matter of the Obligation was not simply and in it self Unlawful, if it had not been so rigorous in excluding all Food, without any exception of Cases of Necessity; and in obliging the People to it under pain of a Curse, and an accursed Death; <ns0:hi>v.</ns0:hi> 38, 39, 44. which was a Punishment far exceeding the Fault.</ns0:note>: so none of the people tasted any food <ns0:note n="p" place="bottom">Partly, in obedience to the Kings Command; and partly, for fear of the Curse.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="25">
                     <ns0:pb facs="tcp:107763:229" />25 And all <ns0:hi>they of</ns0:hi> the land <ns0:note n="q" place="bottom">Heb. <ns0:hi>all the land. i. e.</ns0:hi> The People of the Land; as it is explained below, <ns0:hi>v.</ns0:hi> 30. and so the word is taken, <ns0:hi>Gen.</ns0:hi> 41. 57.                      </ns0:note> came to a wood, and there was honey upon the ground.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="26">26 And when the people were come into the wood, behold, the honey dropped <ns0:note n="r" place="bottom">It hath been observed by many Travellers, and Writers, That Bees do oft-times settle themselves, and make their Hives, and Honey, in the Trunks of Trees, or Clefts of Rocks, or Holes of the Earth; and this in divers Countries, but eminently in this of <ns0:hi>Canaan;</ns0:hi> as may be gathered from <ns0:hi>Deut.</ns0:hi> 32. 13. <ns0:hi>Psal.</ns0:hi> 81. 16. whence it was called, <ns0:hi>a land flowing with milk and honey.</ns0:hi>
                     </ns0:note>, but no man put his hand to his mouth: for the people fear<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ed the oath.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="27">27 But Jonathan heard not <ns0:note n="s" place="bottom">Being then absent, and in pursuit of the <ns0:hi>Philistines,</ns0:hi> di<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />vers of the <ns0:hi>Israelites</ns0:hi> having joyned themselves with him, <ns0:hi>v.</ns0:hi> 21.</ns0:note>, when his father charged the people with the oath: wherefore he put forth the end of the rod that <ns0:hi>was</ns0:hi> in his hand, and dipt it in an honey comb, and put his hand to his mouth, and his eyes were enlightned <ns0:note n="t" place="bottom">He was refreshed, and recovered his lost Spirits, whereof part went into his Optick Nerves, and so cleared his sight, which was much darkned by Famine, as is usual.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="28">28 Then answered one of the people <ns0:note n="u" place="bottom">Who came along with <ns0:hi>Saul,</ns0:hi> whose Forces were now united with <ns0:hi>Ionathan's.</ns0:hi>
                     </ns0:note>, and said, Thy father straitly charged the people with an oath, saying, Cursed <ns0:hi>be</ns0:hi> the man that eateth <ns0:hi>any</ns0:hi> food this day. And the people were <ns0:note n="‖" place="margin">

                        <ns0:hi>i. e.</ns0:hi> The people of the Land, the whole Army, whom by this rash Oath he hath greatly injured.
